# NYCM Friend Finder — Implementation Plan

**Race day:** Sunday, November 1, 2026 · **Plan written:** 2026-10-13 · **~19 days out**

Goal: a throwaway app where a group of friends enter their NYC Marathon start assignment
and transport plan, then browse the roster to find overlaps (same corral, same ferry) on
race morning. Spin up now, tear down after, keep a committed data snapshot in case it's
ever revived.

---

## 1. Decisions locked

| Area | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Hosting | Cloudflare Pages | Free, static + functions in one deploy, `*.pages.dev` URL included |
| Database | Cloudflare D1 (SQLite) | $0, native binding (no connection string/driver), snapshot = one `.sql` file |
| Frontend | Plain HTML + CSS + vanilla JS, no framework | No build step, ~4KB JS, loads fast on a cold phone at 5am on Staten Island |
| API | TypeScript, Cloudflare Pages Functions | Typed server code; wrangler compiles TS natively, no frontend build |
| Access | One shared group passcode (Cloudflare secret) | Keeps strangers out of a public URL; anyone in the group can fix anyone's typo |
| Start time | Derived from wave, not user input | Start time is fully determined by wave — makes `dim_wave` a real conformed dimension instead of a free-text column |
| Transport | Method + assigned departure slot | Method alone puts 8 friends on "the ferry" across a 3-hour window and tells you nothing |
| Deploy | Sam runs wrangler commands | Cloudflare auth stays on Sam's side |

**Running cost: $0.** Pages free tier = unlimited static requests + 100k function
invocations/day. D1 free tier = 5GB storage, 5M row reads/day. Expected usage is ~20
runners and a few hundred page views. Custom domain is the only thing that would ever
cost money (~$10/yr) and `*.pages.dev` is fine for a race-week link.

---

## 2. Verified race facts (seed data)

Confirmed from NYRR for 2026:

- **Start colors: Blue, Orange, Pink.** Green was retired — if you remember green from a
  previous year, it's gone. Three start villages at Fort Wadsworth.
- **Five waves, six corrals per wave** (A–F). Bib shows your wave, color, and corral.
- **Wave start times:**

| Wave | Corrals open | Corrals close | Start |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8:10 AM | 8:45 AM | **9:10 AM** |
| 2 | 9:05 AM | 9:25 AM | **9:45 AM** |
| 3 | 9:45 AM | 10:00 AM | **10:20 AM** |
| 4 | 10:25 AM | 10:40 AM | **10:55 AM** |
| 5 | 11:00 AM | 11:15 AM | **11:30 AM** |

- You may move to a *later/slower* wave or corral, never an earlier one. (This is why the
  fact table keeps history — see §4.)

### Seed data status

NYRR's site is behind a Queue-it waiting room during race week, so seed data came from
secondary sources. It is **data in `migrations/0001_dims.sql`**, not code — correcting a
row is a one-line edit and a migration re-run, no redeploy of app logic.

1. ~~**Bridge level per color.**~~ **RESOLVED 2026-10-14**: blue and orange on the upper
   deck, pink on the lower, corroborated across several 2026 course guides. Seeded as real
   data. Display-only; no matching logic depends on it.
2. **Official transport options — STILL OPEN.** Seeded with the standard set: Staten
   Island Ferry (Whitehall Terminal), NYRR bus from NY Public Library (5th Ave & 42nd St),
   NYRR bus from New Jersey, charity/team bus, own transport/walk — plus two
   partial-knowledge rows added after seeing the real roster (see §11). Departure slot is
   modeled as free 15-minute increments from 4:00 AM to 8:00 AM, which covers every option
   regardless of the official list — deliberately robust to this uncertainty.

**Action for Sam:** when your confirmation email lands, paste the transport options and
I'll correct the seed. The form builds its dropdown from `dim_transport` via `/api/meta`,
so this needs no code change.

## 3. Dimensional model

The honest Kimball read on this: **`fct_runner_start` is a factless fact table.** There are
no additive measures — the table exists to record the co-occurrence of a runner with a
colour, a wave, a corral and a transport plan. That's exactly the Kimball "coverage /
event" pattern, and it's a nice thing to have built one of deliberately.

```
                  dim_color ──┐
                  dim_wave  ──┤
                  dim_corral──┼──> fct_runner_start <── dim_runner
              dim_transport ──┘      (grain: one row per
                                      runner per assignment
                                      version)
```

### Dimensions (all seeded and static except `dim_runner`)

```sql
dim_color     (color_key, color_name, color_hex, village_name, bridge_level, route_note)
dim_wave      (wave_key, wave_num, start_time_local, corral_open, corral_close, wave_label)
dim_corral    (corral_key, corral_letter)
dim_transport (transport_key, transport_label, method, origin_name, origin_borough,
               icon_id, sort_order, is_matchable)
dim_runner    (runner_key, display_name, first_name, last_name)
```

Two things differ from the original plan, both forced by real data (§11):

- `dim_runner.display_name` is **stored, not generated** from `first_name || last_name`.
  Most of the roster is known by a single name, so there is no last name to split out.
  first/last remain optional for anyone who gives both.
- `dim_transport.is_matchable` is 0 for vague answers ("Bus - not sure which", "Still
  deciding"), excluding them from meetup matching. Two shrugs are not a meetup.

### Fact

```sql
fct_runner_start (
  runner_start_key   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
  bib_number         TEXT,              -- degenerate dimension, NULLABLE
  runner_key         INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES dim_runner,   -- the only required one
  color_key          INTEGER REFERENCES dim_color,
  wave_key           INTEGER REFERENCES dim_wave,
  corral_key         INTEGER REFERENCES dim_corral,
  transport_key      INTEGER REFERENCES dim_transport,
  depart_time_local  TEXT,              -- assigned ferry/bus slot, '05:30'
  meetup_note        TEXT,              -- unmodellable by design
  is_current         INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- 1 = live row
  valid_from_utc     TEXT NOT NULL,
  valid_to_utc       TEXT,
  created_at_utc     TEXT NOT NULL,

  CHECK (bib_number IS NULL OR length(trim(bib_number)) > 0),
  CHECK (depart_time_local IS NULL OR depart_time_local GLOB '[0-2][0-9]:[0-5][0-9]'),
  CHECK ((is_current = 1 AND valid_to_utc IS NULL)
      OR (is_current = 0 AND valid_to_utc IS NOT NULL))
)

-- one live row per KNOWN bib (NULLs are each distinct to a unique index)
UNIQUE INDEX ... (bib_number) WHERE is_current = 1 AND bib_number IS NOT NULL
-- one live row per runner: what actually bounds the roster when bibs are unknown
UNIQUE INDEX ... (runner_key) WHERE is_current = 1
```

**Everything except the runner is nullable.** Real sign-up data arrives partial — people
know their wave before their corral, and know they're taking the ferry before anything
else. The original plan's NOT NULLs would have rejected 4 of 19 real entries. See §11.

The `bib_number` non-empty CHECK is load-bearing: `''` is **not** distinct to a unique
index, so three blank bibs would have collided on one index. NULLs coexist fine.

### The one call made on Sam's behalf — flag if you disagree

**The fact table is insert-only with `is_current`** (type-2 style), rather than updating
rows in place. An edit inserts a new row and supersedes the old one.

- Cost: every read needs `WHERE is_current = 1`, which the views handle, so the API never
  sees it.
- Benefit: the committed snapshot becomes a full history — "Sam moved from wave 2 to wave
  3 on Oct 28" is recoverable. Given that NYRR explicitly allows moving to a later wave,
  and that keeping the snapshot is a stated goal, history is worth more here than the
  simplicity of `UPDATE`.

Also deliberately skipped: **no `dim_date`.** For a single-date event it's pure ceremony.

### Views — the app reads only these, never base tables

```sql
v_runner_start     -- denormalized roster, one row per current runner, dims flattened.
                   -- LEFT JOINs + an is_complete flag. The search page's only read.
v_meetup_transport -- tier 1: same vehicle AND same slot
v_meetup_corral    -- tier 2: same color + wave + corral
v_meetup_wave      -- tier 3: same color + wave, any corral
v_meetup_vehicle   -- tier 4: same vehicle, any slot (+ with_times count)
v_roster_gaps      -- who still needs to fill what in
v_start_assignment -- the 3 x 5 x 6 = 90-row cross product, start time pre-joined
```

Keeping all joins in views and the API on `SELECT *` is the separation worth practising —
and it means the "who's with me" logic is SQL, not JavaScript.

`v_runner_start` uses **LEFT JOINs**. With INNER JOINs anyone missing a color, wave or
corral silently vanishes from the roster — worse than useless, since the person most
needing a nudge is the one who disappears.

`v_meetup_wave` and `v_meetup_vehicle` were **not in the original plan**. Both were added
after loading real data showed the planned tiers found almost nobody (§11).

## 4. API surface

`functions/api/` — TypeScript, Pages Functions. All routes except `auth` require
`Authorization: Bearer <token>`.

| Route | Method | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `/api/auth` | POST | `{passcode}` → `{token}`. Constant-time compare, HMAC-signed, 30-day TTL |
| `/api/meta` | GET | Seeded dims + the 17 departure slots, for the form dropdowns |
| `/api/runners` | GET | Whole roster from `v_runner_start`, one shot |
| `/api/runners` | POST | Create (no `runner_key`) or update (with one) |
| `/api/runners/:key` | DELETE | Soft delete — supersedes the live row, keeps history |
| `/api/meetups` | GET | All four match tiers plus the gap list |

**Keyed by `runner_key`, not bib.** The plan said `/api/runners/[bib]`, but bibs became
nullable once real data showed three people without one, so a bib cannot identify a row.

**No server-side filters.** GET returns everything and the page filters client-side: one
request instead of one per keystroke, and it keeps working once loaded — which matters at
5am in a field with 50,000 people on the same cell tower.

**`/api/meta` matters:** form dropdowns are built from the database dimensions, not
hardcoded in HTML. Correcting a seed row fixes the UI with no code change.

**Auth detail:** passcode in, HMAC-signed expiry stamp out (Web Crypto). The **token**
lives in `localStorage`, never the passcode. Stateless — no session table to clean up at
teardown. Constant-time compare that does not leak length. ~60 lines in `lib/auth.ts`.

**Error translation:** SQLite constraint text is mapped to sentences a person can act on —
a duplicate bib reports *whose* bib it is, not an index name.

## 5. Pages

Two pages, shared `app.css` and `app.js`. Card layout, not tables — this gets read on a
phone in the dark. Inline SVG icons only (ferry / bus / car / dot), no icon library, no
dependency, no payload.

**`index.html` — enter your info**
```
Name          [____________]   <- one field. Nicknames are the norm.
Bib #         [____]           <- optional, blank is fine

Start color   ( Blue ) ( Orange ) ( Pink )     <- colored chips
Wave          [ 2 ▾ ]
Corral        [ C ▾ ]
   ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
   │  You start at 9:45 AM           │         <- derived, read-only
   │  Orange village · upper deck    │
   └─────────────────────────────────┘
Getting there [ Staten Island Ferry ▾ ]
Departing     [ 5:30 AM ▾ ]          <- the field nobody fills in; nudge for it
Note (opt.)   [ orange poncho, by Starbucks ]

                        [ Save my info ]
```

**Every field except Name is optional**, and the form must not pretend otherwise — 4 of
19 real entries are missing a colour, wave or corral. One field for the name, not
first/last: most of the roster goes by a single name.

Picking an existing person loads their entry for editing (POST with `runner_key`) rather
than creating a duplicate. Bib is not an identifier — three people don't have one.

**`search.html` — the roster, tiered and wave-led**

Match tiers render strongest-first, and a tier with no rows is hidden entirely. On real
data that means the corral and wave tiers carry the page while the exact slot tier is
empty — see §11. It lights up on its own as people add departure times.

```
▸ SAME CORRAL
   🏁 Pink · Wave 1 · B — Runner J, Runner R

▸ SAME VILLAGE + WAVE
   🏁 Orange · Wave 1 · 9:10 — you, Runner A (B), Runner F (D)
   🏁 Pink   · Wave 4 · 10:55 — Runner W (?), Runner K (C), Runner X (A)

▸ ALSO ON THE FERRY  (time unknown)
   🚢 7 people — only 2 said when. Compare notes?

[ search name or bib_____ ]
( All ) ( Blue ) ( Orange ) ( Pink )  ( Wave ▾ ) ( Transport ▾ )

● Runner C           #9xxxx
  Orange · Wave 1 · Corral C · 9:10 AM
  🚢 Staten Island Ferry 5:30 AM

● Runner W                   #9xxxx
  Pink · Wave 4 · Corral — · 10:55 AM        ⚠ needs info
  🚌 Charity / team bus 6:00 AM

● Runner A        —
  — · — · —                                  ⚠ needs info
  🚢 Staten Island Ferry
```

Full roster visible by default — with ~20 friends you browse, not search. The box filters
client-side from one `/api/runners` fetch; no round-trip per keystroke.

Incomplete entries stay visible with a muted `—` and a `⚠ needs info` badge, driven by
`is_complete` from the view. Hiding them would hide the people most worth nudging.

| 2 | API | Five endpoints, verified with curl against local D1 | **DONE** 10-14 |

**Resume here:** soft launch is live and a few friends are testing. Next real step is the
wider send, once the transport options are confirmed (§2). See §16 for live details.

### Commands Sam runs (phase 4)

```bash
npx wrangler login
npx wrangler d1 create nycm-friendfinder          # paste the returned ID into wrangler.toml
npx wrangler d1 migrations apply nycm-friendfinder --remote
npx wrangler pages project create nycm-friendfinder
npx wrangler pages secret put GROUP_PASSCODE --project-name nycm-friendfinder
npx wrangler pages secret put TOKEN_SECRET --project-name nycm-friendfinder
npm run deploy                                    # stamps version.json, then deploys
```

**Then, in the dashboard, once per zone:** Caching → Configuration → Browser Cache TTL →
**Respect Existing Headers**. A new zone defaults to 4 hours and silently overrides
`public/_headers` for `.js` and `.css` — that is the "I have to clear my cache to see
updates" bug, and `_headers` alone does not fix it. See §17.

Local dev needs none of the above — `npx wrangler pages dev public` with a local SQLite D1.

## 8. Teardown and revival

```bash
# Snapshot — do this BEFORE deleting anything
npx wrangler d1 export nycm-friendfinder --remote --output=snapshots/nycm2026-final.sql
git add snapshots/ && git commit -m "Final 2026 race-day data snapshot"

# Tear down
npx wrangler pages project delete nycm-friendfinder
npx wrangler d1 delete nycm-friendfinder
```

Revival is `d1 create` + `d1 execute --file=snapshots/nycm2026-final.sql` + `npm run
deploy`, plus resetting Browser Cache TTL to "Respect Existing Headers" on whatever zone
it lands on (§7, §17) — that one is not in the repo and a fresh zone defaults it wrong.
Because the snapshot is a plain `.sql` file in the repo, it also loads straight into local
SQLite, DuckDB or Postgres for analysis without any Cloudflare account at all — which is
probably how it'll actually get used a year from now.

## 11. Phase 1 complete — 2026-10-14

Scaffold, schema, seed and loader all built and verified against a local D1.

### What the real roster CSV changed

Loading 19 real entries exposed that the schema assumed complete data and real sign-up
data is not. Migrations `0001`–`0003` were **rewritten in place** rather than patched with
an `0004`, because they had only ever run against a throwaway local database — the rule
against editing applied migrations protects *deployed* ones.

- **Everything except the runner is now nullable.** One person (ferry only, no colour,
  wave or corral) would have been silently dropped by the original INNER JOINs. Views use
  LEFT JOINs and expose `is_complete` to drive a "needs info" badge.
- **`bib_number` got a non-empty CHECK.** Three blank bibs arrived as `''`, which is *not*
  distinct to a unique index, so all three would have collided on the live-bib index.
  NULLs coexist; empty strings do not. Loader writes NULL.
- **`dim_runner` stores `display_name` directly** instead of generating it from
  `first_name || ' ' || last_name`. 13 of 19 people are known by a single name — there is
  no last name to split out, and inventing one is worse than not having it.
- **`dim_transport` gained `is_matchable`**, set to 0 for "Bus - not sure which" and
  "Still deciding". Two people who both shrugged are not a meetup.

### The finding that reorders the product

Slot-matching — the field argued for hardest during planning — **finds nobody on the real
roster.** Only 3 of 19 gave a departure time and all three differ.

| Tier | View | Matches on 19 real rows |
|---|---|---|
| Exact | `v_meetup_transport` (vehicle + slot) | **0** |
| Strong | `v_meetup_corral` (colour + wave + corral) | **1** pair |
| Good | `v_meetup_wave` (colour + wave) | **7 groups, 16 of 19 people** |
| Loose | `v_meetup_vehicle` (vehicle, any time) | **7** on the ferry (2 with times) |

So the search page is **tiered and wave-led**: corral → wave/village → vehicle. The exact
tier stays in the schema and lights up on its own as people fill times in. `v_meetup_wave`
and `v_meetup_vehicle` were both added after seeing the data; neither was in the original
plan.

### Roster data handling

The CSV is **gitignored** (`*.csv`), as is the generated `seed/` SQL. Real names plus bib
numbers are enough to look someone up on NYRR tracking, and the repo — though private
today — is meant to hold a long-lived snapshot. The loader is committed; the data is not.

```bash
npm run roster:build -- am_ftc_athletes_nycm.csv   # CSV -> seed/roster_load.sql
npm run db:load:local                              # -> local D1
```

Re-running is a reset-and-load, local only.

### Also fixed

- `@cloudflare/workers-types` v4 → v5 (wrangler 4.151 peer requirement)
- `typescript` was never installed; added with a `typecheck` script
- `npm run typecheck` reports "no inputs found" until Phase 2 writes the first `.ts`

## 12. Phase 2 complete — 2026-10-14

Five endpoints as Pages Functions, reading views only. `tsc --noEmit` clean.
Shared server code lives in `lib/` — deliberately outside `functions/`, where every file
becomes a route.

### Verified end to end against local D1

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| No token | 401 `missing passcode` |
| Wrong passcode | 401 |
| Token with one byte flipped | 401 — HMAC holds |
| `GET /api/runners` | 19 rows, `NULLS LAST` puts the empty entry last |
| `"5:30 AM"` in the time field | readable error naming the format |
| Departure time with no vehicle | rejected — a time for nothing |
| Duplicate bib | 409, names *whose* bib it is |
| Create with partial info | 201, `is_complete = 0` |
| Edit → move wave | new row live, old row closed with a timestamp |
| Soft delete | roster 20→19, **both history rows kept**, second delete 404s |
| `GET /api/meetups` | 4 tiers + 13-person gap list |

### Decisions made during Phase 2

- **Entries key on `runner_key`, not bib.** Forced by nullable bibs (§11).
- **No server-side filters.** One GET, client-side filtering. Fewer moving parts and it
  survives a bad cell connection at the start village.
- **30-day token TTL.** Nobody should be typing a passcode at 4am.
- **Validation messages over constraint strings.** The DB CHECKs remain the backstop, but
  a person gets a sentence they can act on.

### Fixed mid-phase

Typing `5:30 AM` reported *"too long (max 5)"* because the length check ran before the
format check. The format check now owns the message.

### Known cosmetic issue

None outstanding. `npm run typecheck` is clean now that `functions/` and `lib/` have
files — the "no inputs found" error noted in §11 is gone.

## 14. Phase 3 complete — UI, 2026-10-14

Two pages, five client modules, no framework and no build step. Dark mode follows the OS.

- `index.html` + `browse.js` — roster, match tiers, saved people, filters
- `me.html` + `me.js` — edit your own entry, also the re-add page
- `gate.js` — password → claim / sign in / onboard
- `form.js` — the entry form, shared by onboarding and editing
- `app.js` — tokens, fetch, icons, formatting

### Bugs found by simulating an empty production database

Local always had 19 imported runners, which hid all of these:

- **Ghost sign-in.** A valid token for a deleted runner walked past the gate into a dead
  state — no card, no edit link, nothing but sign out. Reachable in production via a PIN
  reset or a redeployed database. `requireProfile` now checks the runner exists and 401s.
- **"Take me off the roster" was a one-way door.** The edit link hid exactly when it was
  needed. Both pages now treat a missing row as "add me back" and reuse the same form.
- **Empty claim screen lied** — "everyone on the spreadsheet has already set a PIN" is
  nonsense on a fresh deploy where no spreadsheet exists.

### The match tiers were rebuilt

The original group-wide tiers were **not about you**. `v_meetup_corral` and friends find
clusters anywhere in the roster, so "Same corral" headed a list of corrals you were not
in. They were also inert — members arrived as a `GROUP_CONCAT` string, so a suggested name
could not be starred without scrolling off to find them again.

Replaced with **"People near you"**: overlap computed client-side, since the browser
already holds the roster and knows who you are. Each match is a real runner object, so it
is a normal card with a normal star. The views remain for analysis in `sql/`.

Ranking is one combined ladder — same ride+time > same corral > same village+wave > same
ride > same village — with ties broken by how much else is shared. Every comparison guards
both sides for null first: in JS `null === null` is true, so two people who both have no
corral would otherwise read as sharing one.

## 17. Cache busting — 2026-10-16

**Feedback:** "when updates get pushed to production, I don't see them until I clear my
cache in my browser."

**Cause.** Cloudflare Pages serves static assets with `Cache-Control: public,
max-age=14400` by default. The HTML was already `max-age=0, must-revalidate`, which is
what made this confusing to diagnose: the *page* was always fresh, and every line of
actual behaviour — `browse.js`, `me.js`, `app.js`, `form.js`, `gate.js`, `app.css` — was up
to four hours stale. A deploy looked like it had landed and had not.

**Fix 1 — `public/_headers`.** Static assets now revalidate, one **exact path** per
asset: `/`, `/me`, `/app.css`, `/app.js`, `/browse.js`, `/form.js`, `/gate.js`, `/me.js`,
`/version.json`.

`no-cache` is not `no-store`. The browser keeps the file and asks the edge whether it
changed; unchanged is a 304 with no body, answered from Cloudflare's edge rather than
the origin. The whole frontend is ~30 KB, so this trades a round trip for never being
stale — the right side of that trade when there is no build step and no hashed filenames.

**Exact paths are not a style choice — they are the only form that works.** The first
version of this file used `/*.js`, `/*.css` and `/*.html`. `wrangler pages dev` parses
those, says "Parsed 5 valid header rules" and serves `no-cache` for them. **The production
edge ignores them and says nothing.** The deploy succeeded and changed nothing: every
module still answered `max-age=14400`.

What disguised it: `/index.html` and `/me.html` answer **308**, and the redirect carried
`no-cache`, so a quick check looked like it had worked. The pages themselves (`/` and
`/me`) and all six modules had not. A splat seems to have to be the last thing in a
pattern; a mid-pattern one matches nothing, silently.

A blanket `/*` does work, but `_headers` **appends** to what a Pages Function already
sent, so it made `/api/*` come back `Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store`. The API's own
`no-store` (in `lib/http.ts`) is the stronger and correct answer for a private roster of
real names and bibs, so exact paths are also what leaves the Functions routes alone.
Verified: `/api/meta` still answers `no-store` alone.

Because exact paths mean a new module needs a new rule — and a missing rule fails the same
silent way — `npm run deploy` now checks `_headers` against `public/` and **exits non-zero
if any asset has no rule**, accounting for Pages serving `foo.html` at `/foo`. Verified it
catches a removed rule and aborts the deploy.

**There was a second, independent cause — and it was not in the repo at all.** After the
exact-path deploy, `/` `/me` and `/version.json` obeyed `_headers` on the custom domain
while every `.js` and `.css` still came back `max-age=14400`. The split is the tell:

```
                 .pages.dev        nycm26friendfinder.com
/app.js          no-cache  ✓       max-age=14400   cf-cache-status: REVALIDATED
/version.json    no-cache  ✓       no-cache        cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC
```

`_headers` was already correct — proven on `.pages.dev`, where everything obeyed it. The
custom domain's **Cloudflare zone** was overriding it: **Caching → Configuration → Browser
Cache TTL**, sitting at Cloudflare's default of **4 hours**. It rewrites `Cache-Control`
only for the extensions Cloudflare caches at the edge, which is why `.js`/`.css`
(`REVALIDATED`) were overridden and HTML/`.json` (`DYNAMIC`) were not.

Fixed by setting Browser Cache TTL to **Respect Existing Headers** (dashboard, no deploy).
**This setting is not in the repo.** A fresh Cloudflare zone for this project starts at 4
hours again, and `_headers` alone will not save it. It belongs in the teardown/revival
checklist (§8) and in any rebuild.

Both causes produced the identical number, 14400, because Pages' asset default and
Cloudflare's zone default are both 4 hours. That is why fixing one looked like fixing
nothing.

**The lesson worth keeping.** `wrangler pages dev` is more permissive than the edge, and
the custom domain is not the same thing as `.pages.dev`. For anything that is a *hosting*
behaviour rather than app logic — headers, redirects, routes — local dev passing is not
evidence. Check the live URL, and when the custom domain and `.pages.dev` disagree, the
difference is zone configuration, not code. Comparing the two hostnames would have found
this before the first deploy instead of after the third.

**Fix 2 — reload a tab that is already open.** Headers fix the next visit and do nothing
for a phone with the roster tab open for days, which is the actual race-morning shape.
`scripts/stamp_version.mjs` writes `public/version.json` at deploy time, and
`watchForUpdates()` in `app.js` compares it when the tab comes back into view:

- Same build → nothing happens.
- New build → `location.reload()`, which now gets fresh code because of Fix 1.
- New build but work in progress → **holds**, and reloads at the next opportunity
  instead. The roster vetoes on an active search or filter; `me.html` vetoes on a form
  with any typed input. Losing a half-filled form to a deploy would be a worse bug than
  the one being fixed.

The build id is a hash of the frontend's own bytes, not the git SHA, because every deploy
here is manual and may run against a dirty tree — a commit-based id would miss changes
that are live. A redeploy of identical files keeps its id and does not reload anyone.

**Verified in a browser against local dev**, all four paths: new build reloads; new build
with a search active does not and the typed text survives; clearing the search then
reloads; new build with a dirty form does not. Also confirmed `_headers` itself is not
served, and that both pages still boot. Fix 2 is app logic, so local dev *is* evidence for
it — unlike Fix 1.

**Confirmed working on production, 10-16.** All nine assets answer `no-cache` on the
custom domain, `/api/meta` answers `no-store` alone, and revalidation is doing what it was
supposed to: a conditional request with the current ETag returns **304 with no body**, a
stale one returns 200 with the full 4,918 bytes. The live site boots, all four modules
load, and the watcher fetches `version.json`.

**Live check after any deploy that touches this:**

```bash
curl -sI https://nycm26friendfinder.com/app.js | grep -i cache-control   # want: no-cache
curl -s  https://nycm26friendfinder.com/version.json                     # want: the build you just stamped
```

**The trap to remember.** `version.json` is only as good as the last stamp. Deploy with
`npm run deploy`, not bare `wrangler pages deploy`, or open tabs stop noticing new builds
— silently, since nothing errors.

## 18. Making the fields visible — 2026-10-16

**Feedback:** "is there a way to bring attention to the input and dropdown fields? It feels
like the boxes could easily get missed."

**Cause, straight out of the CSS.** A field and the card around it were the same colour
with the same hairline border:

```
.card    background: var(--card)   border: 1px solid var(--line)
input    background: var(--card)   border: 1px solid var(--line)
```

`#ffffff` on `#ffffff` in light, `#17191e` on `#17191e` in dark. And `appearance: none`
stripped the native dropdown arrow without replacing it, so **five of the eight fields
were dropdowns that looked exactly like text inputs** — nothing said that tapping
"Departure time" opens twenty choices.

**Fixed with four signals, not one** — the same lesson as the colour chips:

1. **Recessed fill.** Fields use `--bg`: greyer than the card in light, darker in dark, so
   a field reads as a well either way.
2. **`--field-line`, a much stronger border**, holding ~3:1 against the card *and* the page
   background. This is what actually carries it — the roster's search box sits directly on
   `--bg`, where the fill shows nothing and the outline is the only thing making it a box.
   `--line` stays what it was: a card edge you should barely notice.
3. **A chevron on every select**, as a background-image, so no markup changed. It is a
   per-theme token because a data URI cannot take `currentColor`. Note the field rule sets
   `background-color`, not the shorthand — the shorthand would wipe the chevron out
   depending on rule order.
4. **Unanswered dropdowns are muted**, and disabled ones look disabled. "— not sure yet —"
   rendered in full text colour, so a form with nothing in it looked as complete as a form
   with everything. Muting shows what is left without scolding: blank is a legitimate
   answer here and stays one.

**Verified in the browser in both themes**, on the form and the roster. The search box is
the case worth re-checking if these values are ever touched: its fill is identical to the
page behind it, so only the border makes it a box.

**Still device-driven only.** `prefers-color-scheme` plus `<meta name="color-scheme">`.
The `[data-theme]` hooks exist in the CSS and nothing sets them — handy for testing both
themes from the console, not a feature.

## 19. Accessibility pass — 2026-10-16

WCAG 2.2 AA audit of both pages. Eleven real defects. Everything below was either
measured with a contrast calculator or checked in the browser's accessibility tree — none
of it was assumed.

**Missing names and relationships (1.3.1, 3.3.2, 4.1.2)**

- Roster search was labelled by its **placeholder alone** — not a label, and it vanishes
  as soon as you type. Now `aria-label`.
- "Start colour" was a bare `<label>` with no `for`, above a div of buttons — a label
  attached to nothing. Chips are now a labelled `role="group"`.
- PIN rules, departure-time hint and the "exactly as you typed it" note floated after
  their fields with no association. Now `aria-describedby`.

**State carried only by colour (1.3.1, 4.1.2)**

- Active filters were a background colour plus a CSS class. A screen reader user could not
  tell the list was already narrowed. Now `aria-pressed`, with both filter rows as labelled
  groups. (The star already had `aria-pressed` and a proper label — that one was fine.)

**Things that happened silently (4.1.3)**

- Filtering/searching rewrites the list with no announcement. There is now a live region
  reporting "N of M people match". **It lives in the page shell, not inside `#app`** —
  `#app` is replaced wholesale on every render, and a live region that gets replaced does
  not reliably announce. Verified the node survives a re-render.
- The derived "You start at 9:10 AM" box updates as you pick colour and wave → `role="status"`.
- Every error (wrong password, mismatched PIN, failed save) appeared with no announcement
  → `role="alert"`.

**Contrast, measured (1.4.11, 1.4.3)**

| | was | now | need |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--field-line` on card (light) | 2.91:1 | **3.31:1** | 3.0 |
| `--field-line` on page (light) | 2.72:1 | **3.09:1** | 3.0 |
| saved star on card (light) | 1.92:1 | **4.92:1** | 3.0 |
| `--muted` on page (light) | 4.51:1 | **5.40:1** | 4.5 |

The field border I shipped yesterday **looked** right and was under the line — that is
exactly why it needs calculating. Dark mode already passed everything. The star keeps
`#eab308` in dark (9:1); darkening it there would have made it worse. Its state was never
colour-alone — filled vs outline shape already carried it — so this was a contrast fix,
not a 1.4.1 fix.

**Target size (2.5.8, 24×24):** star 27px → 33×35. Header link 20px tall → 30. Vertical
padding on an *inline* element grows the hit box without moving the baseline, so nothing
shifted.

**Also:** "Add me back" was a `<button>` nested inside an `<a>` — invalid, and two
overlapping controls for one action. Now the link alone, styled as the ghost button it was
imitating. And `:focus-visible` now covers buttons, links and chips, which had been falling
back to the browser default; verified the ring is legible on a *filled* colour chip, the
one place it had to be.

**Verified:** zero unnamed controls on either page, every field resolves to a real
accessible name, heading order h1 → h2, no target under 24px, live region updates and
survives re-render, focus ring appears on keyboard Tab.

**What was already right** and did not need touching: `lang`, distinct page titles, the
`<main>` landmark, heading order, star `aria-label`/`aria-pressed`, `aria-hidden` on
decorative icons, colour never used alone (every dot and chip has text beside it), no
animation, pinch-zoom not blocked, single-column reflow.

**Deliberately not done.** Empty fields are muted grey, not flagged as needing attention.
The page says "Blank is fine" and four of nineteen real entries genuinely do not know their
corral. Making unanswered fields look like errors would be a product decision, not an
accessibility one.

## 20. Privacy model for ~1000 users — proposal, 2026-10-16

Written when Sam raised opening the app to his network and the networks of current users
via social media, est. max ~1000 signups. **Not implemented. This is a decision document.**

Every risk accepted in §16 "Known and accepted" is justified there by *"a 19-person app
with a three-week life."* Social media removes that sentence. The accepted risks were
choices, not oversights — but they were choices made against a premise that no longer
holds, so they need re-making, not re-justifying.

### What one roster row exposes today

`display_name`, `bib_number`, start colour / village, wave, corral, start time,
transport, `depart_time_local`, `meetup_note` (free text). `/api/runners` returns the
whole table to anyone with a profile.

Two properties that are already right and should be preserved:

- **Stars are private.** `/api/saved` is scoped `WHERE runner_key = ?`, so nobody can see
  who has saved them. Keep it that way.
- **The roster needs a profile, not just the passcode.** You must add yourself before you
  can see anyone. That raises the cost of casual scraping — though not of a determined
  person, who simply creates an entry.

### What changes at 1000

The passcode circulates by screenshot and DM; assume it is public. Then the app is a
searchable index of ~1000 named runners, their bib numbers, and **the exact minute and
place each of them will physically be**, mostly before dawn. `meetup_note` is worse than
it looks — "orange poncho, by the Starbucks" is a physical description plus a location.

The repo's own `.gitignore` already says *"A name + bib is enough to look someone up on
NYRR tracking."* That reasoning was applied to a 19-person CSV. It applies harder here.

Among 16 friends consent is implicit. Among 1000 strangers it is not, and the people most
exposed by a pre-dawn location feed are not the ones who will think to object.

### The decision that has to reverse

§14 records that overlap is computed **client-side**, deliberately: *"the only thing the
server could add is a round trip."* That was right for a roster everyone was entitled to
see in full.

**You cannot withhold a field from the client and still match on it in the client.** Any
tiered-visibility model forces matching to the server. This is the main engineering cost
of everything below, and it is worth noting it also *helps* the 1000-row performance
problem: the server returns matches and a thin directory instead of the whole table.

### Options

**1. Mutual-star detail — recommended.**
Visible to everyone: name, start village/colour, wave. Enough to spot someone you know.
Visible only once you have *both* starred each other: bib, corral, transport, departure
time, note. Suggestions still appear for non-mutual pairs, but as a tier label ("same wave
+ ride") with no underlying values. The product still does its job: find your friend,
both confirm, then see exactly where to meet.

**2. Per-user visibility setting.** Everyone / only people I've starred / village + wave
only. Cheaper, keeps client-side matching for whoever opts into "everyone". But defaults
decide everything, and a mixed roster confuses people ("why can't I see Dana's time?").

**3. No global roster.** Search by name or bib you already know, plus server-computed
suggestions. Strongest privacy and it solves the unbrowsable-1000-rows problem outright.
Biggest product change.

**Why 1.** At 1000, "find your friends" inverts. With 16 people you browse everyone; with
1000 strangers you want the three people you already know. **The global browsable roster
becomes less useful and more dangerous at the same time** — so the privacy fix and the
scale fix are the same fix. Option 1 converges on option 3 anyway: once detail is
mutual-only, "Everyone" is a thin name + village + wave directory, cheap to paginate and
low-risk to expose.

### Do regardless of which option

| | Why | Effort |
|---|---|---|
| Drop `bib_number` from roster display | Highest-risk field, and display is only a convenience — sign-in still needs it | Small |
| `meetup_note` opt-in + mutual-only | It is a physical description of a person in the dark | Small |
| Rate limit `/api/auth` and `/api/profile/signin` | None today. A 4-digit PIN is 10,000 guesses; unthrottled that is minutes, and the prize is editing someone's start info | Small — Cloudflare dashboard rules, no code |
| Real delete, not hide | "Take me off the roster" keeps the row. Fine among friends; with strangers, delete should delete | Small |
| One line at onboarding: what is collected, who sees it | Needed the moment strangers join | Small |
| Per-invite codes instead of one shared passcode | Lets you revoke one leak without resetting everybody | Medium |
| **Do not commit the final snapshot to git** | §8 teardown says `git add snapshots/`. At 19 friends that is a keepsake; at 1000 it is a thousand strangers' names and bibs in a repo | Change the plan, not the code |

### Not addressed here

Roster performance at 1000 rows (`SELECT *` with no LIMIT; `innerHTML` rebuild on every
keystroke), and D1 free-tier read volume. Both are real and both are in §19's sequencing
note, but they are engineering, not consent.

still a soft launch among friends. §16 remains the production reference; §13 is superseded
by this section.

### Done since the last resume point

| | Section |
|---|---|

Commits: `534f1fd`, `de4de34`, `9ec8de0`, `1228f82`, `9e56cd9`, `8921d4d`.

### Transport — shipped

Migration `0005_transport_from_nyrr.sql`, applied to production and verified: 16
assignments intact, zero orphans. The live dropdown is now, in order:

```
Staten Island Ferry             matchable     13 people
New Jersey Bus (Meadowlands)    matchable      0
Midtown Bus (NYPL)              matchable      0
Have My Own Transportation      NOT matchable  0
Charity / team bus              matchable      2  (Fritz, Rena / Reeny)
Bus - not sure which            NOT matchable  0
Still deciding                  NOT matchable  1
```

No redeploy was needed — the form builds this from the database via `/api/meta`, which is
the property §2 was designed for and the first time it has actually paid out.

Pre-migration backup was written to the session scratchpad, which is **gone now**. If a
future migration needs one, `npx wrangler d1 export nycm-friendfinder --remote --output=<path>`
and put it somewhere that survives.

### Open decision 1 — is "Charity / team bus" matchable?

It currently is. The question: two people on *different* charities' buses are not
travelling together, so matching them sends them to different pickups. The same reasoning
already makes "Bus - not sure which" unmatchable, and 0005 applied it to "Have My Own
Transportation".

Right now **Fritz has no departure time and Rena has 05:00**, so no exact match exists
between them yet — it would appear the moment Fritz picks a time.

**Cheapest resolution: ask those two which charity they are with.** Same charity → leave it
matchable, no code. Different → set `is_matchable = 0` in a one-line migration. Two people
is a question answerable faster than any feature.

### Open decision 2 — the charity picker, only if the app widens

Design agreed in principle, **not built**. Pick "Charity / team bus" → a second dropdown of
charities already entered → "Mine isn't listed" → text box. Charities become rows in
`dim_transport`, so matching needs **no new logic** — same-charity riders share a
`transport_key` exactly like ferry riders.

Drift control, which was Sam's concern and the right one:

- Normalise on write (lowercase, trim, collapse whitespace, strip punctuation) and reuse
  an existing row rather than inserting a near-duplicate. Catches `Team for Kids` /
  `team for kids` / `Team  For Kids `.
- Does **not** catch `TFK` vs `Team for Kids`. Nothing does. The defence is showing the
  existing list first so picking beats typing.
- At ~1000 users, **seed NYRR's official charity partner list** rather than starting empty,
  or the write-in becomes the primary path and the list rots within a week.

Cost ≈ 60–100 lines: a migration, a resolve-or-create endpoint, and the conditional second
control in `form.js`. Plus a runtime-growing dimension on a live database with no admin
screen — a typo'd charity sits in everyone's dropdown until fixed by hand with
`db:q:remote`.

**Do not build this for 2 charity riders.** Build it if charity becomes a real cluster,
say five or more, where asking people individually stops scaling.

### Open decision 3 — the privacy model, if opening to ~1000

Full proposal in **§20**. The short version:

- Every risk accepted in §16 is justified there by *"a 19-person app with a three-week
  life."* Social media removes that sentence. Those were choices, not oversights — but the
  premise changed, so they need re-making.
- Recommended: **mutual-star detail** (§20 option 1). Everyone sees name + village + wave;
  bib, corral, transport, departure time and note appear only once two people have both
  starred each other.
- **The one architectural consequence:** §14 made overlap client-side deliberately. You
  cannot withhold a field from the client and still match on it there, so any tiered model
  forces matching onto the server. That also helps the 1000-row performance problem.
- **Do regardless, even if the app never widens:** rate limiting (there is none anywhere
  today — a 4-digit PIN is 10,000 unthrottled guesses) and dropping `bib_number` from the
  roster display. Both small, both reduce exposure now.
- **Flagged hardest:** §8 teardown says `git add snapshots/`. At 19 friends that is a
  keepsake; at 1000 it is a thousand strangers' names and bib numbers committed to a repo.
  Easy to do on autopilot in three weeks. Decide before then.

### Suggested order when picking this back up

1. Ask Fritz and Rena about the charity bus — one message, closes decision 1.
2. Rate limiting + drop bib from display — small, worth doing even at 19 people.
3. Only if actually widening: §20 privacy model, then roster performance, then the charity
   picker.

### Not addressed anywhere yet

Roster performance at scale. `/api/runners` is `SELECT * FROM v_runner_start` with no
LIMIT, and `render()` rebuilds every card through `innerHTML` **on every keystroke** in the
search box. Fine at 16, visibly janky at 1000. Also unchecked: D1 free-tier read volume at
1000 users × 1000 rows × several loads each.

### The pattern that has held all week

Every genuine UI bug this project has had came from Sam or a tester, not from my own
testing — the cache staleness, the invisible fields, the colour chip. Two corrections this
session came from checking live production rather than local dev or my own judgement:
`wrangler pages dev` honoured header rules the real edge ignores, and a field border I had
called "roughly 3:1" measured 2.91. **Keep the tester loop short, and check the live URL
rather than the local one for anything that is hosting behaviour rather than app logic.**

**Feedback:** "I like that each person has their colour dot, their name and their bib
number — I don't like how 'unreadable' the 2nd line looks. Is it possible to put
colour/wave/corral in little badges instead of being separated by dots? I want to make
sure that everybody's info is easily scannable and eye-catching upon glance."

**Light/dark — checked first, nothing to fix.** `prefers-color-scheme` plus
`<meta name="color-scheme">` on both pages, nothing sets `[data-theme]`, no toggle and no
stored preference. Verified in the browser rather than read off the CSS: with the OS in
dark the body computes `#0d0e11`, forcing `[data-theme=light]` gives `#f7f7f8`, and
removing it returns to the OS value. The form page is the one that matters for the other
half of this — native select popups and the caret follow the document colour-scheme from
the meta tag — and it renders fully dark. It already matched the machine.

### The actual diagnosis

The second line was `.meta`: `--muted`, 14px, dot-separated.

```
Orange · Wave 1 · Corral C · 9:10 AM
```

Two separate things were wrong and only one of them is the dots.

1. **It was muted, and it is the most important content on the card.** The roster exists
   to answer "where is this person starting"; that line is the answer, rendered in the
   colour reserved for things you can ignore. The name and the bib — which you already
   know, because you went looking for them — were the only full-contrast text.
2. **A sentence has to be read; a badge can be matched.** The facts in that line are the
   exact values you compare against your own. Run together in one string, every card costs
   a left-to-right read. As discrete blocks in fixed positions, a column of cards can be
   pattern-matched without reading any of them.

### What shipped

```
● Runner C  you  #9xxxx                              ★
  [Orange] [Wave 1] [Corral C]              starts 9:10 AM
  [🚢 Staten Island Ferry]                  leaves 5:30 AM
```

- **One badge geometry for everything on the card** — info, overlap tag, needs-info — so
  only colour separates their jobs and the card reads as one system.
- **The start colour badge is filled with the start colour**, reusing the form's colour
  chip recipe exactly, so "Orange" looks the same wherever it appears in the app.
- **All three start slots always render.** An unanswered one is a dashed muted badge
  holding its position (`Corral —`), so badges line up vertically across cards and a gap
  is a gap in a fixed place rather than a shorter row. Dashed matches `.derived`, which is
  the same "nothing here yet" idea. Never red — §19's rule that blank is a legitimate
  answer still holds, and four of nineteen real entries genuinely do not know their corral.
  When nothing at all is known it collapses to one `Start info —` badge rather than three.
- **Times are right-aligned into a column** and keyed `starts` / `leaves`. The key word is
  load-bearing in two ways: a card carries a start time and a departure time, and without
  it they are told apart only by which row they are in — and it is the only thing a screen
  reader gets, which otherwise hears two bare clock times per card.
- **The transport icon kept its 15px**, at a heavier 1.95 stroke inside a badge so the
  ferry's mast and the bus's wheels survive next to 600-weight text.

### Contrast, measured before writing the CSS

The badge surface needed a place in the boundary ladder §18 established. It is not a tap
target, so it must not out-shout a field; it is not a card edge, so it must be more
visible than one.

| vs the card | | light | dark |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--line` | card edge, barely noticeable | 1.27:1 | 1.28:1 |
| `--pill-line` | **badge, new** | **1.69:1** | **1.77:1** |
| `--tag-line` | **overlap tag, new** | **2.27:1** | **2.29:1** |
| `--field-line` | tap target, must not be missed | 3.31:1 | 3.21:1 |

Text on the badge fill is 14.7:1 light / 11.9:1 dark. White on the three start colours
darkened 85% is orange **4.73:1**, pink 6.01, blue 6.64 — orange is the tightest and the
one to re-measure if a seeded hex ever changes. Both new tokens are within 0.02 of their
opposite-theme twin, so a badge carries the same weight in both themes.

**The overlap tag was the one thing I got wrong on the first pass.** It started with
`border-color: var(--accent)`, reusing `.card.me`'s "this one is yours" signal. In dark
mode `--accent` is near-white, which made the tag the loudest thing on the card and beat
the person's own name — the section heading already says these people overlap with you,
so the tag only has to say how. Caught by looking at it, not by reading the CSS.

### Two things the redesign exposed

- **"needs info" on a card with no visible gap.** Once gaps render as dashed slots, a card
  showing all three slots filled and still flagged incomplete looks like it is complaining
  about nothing. `is_complete` is bib + colour + wave + corral, so when the three start
  slots are filled the only thing it can mean is the bib. The badge now says **"needs
  bib"** in that case. (Worth remembering that §21 proposes dropping bib from the roster
  display for privacy — that would make this branch dead code.)
- **Badges joined on `''` read as "OrangeWave 2"** to assistive tech that flattens
  adjacent inline text. Joined on a space instead; flex ignores whitespace between items,
  so the layout is byte-identical. Verified both: badge positions unchanged, and the card
  now speaks "Blue Wave 3 Corral D starts 10:20 AM Staten Island Ferry leaves 6:45 AM".

### Verified in the browser

Both themes. All three start colours. The complete card, the partial gap (`Corral —`), the
total gap (`Start info —`), and a card with no transport row at all. Search still filters,
and focus and caret still survive the re-render it does on every keystroke. The live region
still announces "1 of 18 people match".

**Width is the thing to re-check if these values are ever touched.** The worst case is the
longest colour plus a two-digit start time — `[Orange] [Wave 3] [Corral C] starts 10:20 AM`
— which measures **303px against the 313px** a card has inside it on a 375px phone. It
fits without wrapping, with 10px to spare. Below about 340px the time wraps to its own
right-aligned line, which is the intended degradation, not a break.

### Not done

Not committed and not deployed — the working tree holds `app.css`, `app.js`, `browse.js`.
`startLine()` is gone from `app.js`, replaced by `startFacts()`; nothing else imported it.

## 23. Tightening "people near you" — 2026-10-28

**Feedback:** "Change the logic to be same wave, and only same transportation if the
transport time is the same… just because I'm taking the ferry and someone else is taking
the ferry, but they're 2 hrs apart, don't label them as 'near me'. I basically want to be
able to use this app to see if friends can find friends the morning of the marathon."

That last sentence is the spec. The §14 ladder answered a looser question — "do you have
anything in common" — and tagged the answer with the same confident label as a real match.

### The two rungs doing the damage

- **`same ride`, vehicle only.** Departure slots run 04:00–08:30 (§15). Two people on the
  Staten Island Ferry could be four and a half hours apart and still be called near each
  other. This was the single worst signal in the app.
- **`same village`, colour only, across any wave.** Wave 1 starts 9:10 and wave 5 starts
  11:30 — the same two-hour problem wearing different clothes.

Both were *added* in §11 precisely because the strict tiers found nobody on the imported
roster. That was the right call against that data and the wrong one against this product:
the fix for an empty list was to loosen what counts as a match, which fills the list with
leads that do not pay out. §16 already noted the tier ordering should be re-checked once
the roster had real departure times in it. This is that re-check.

### The ladder now

Two occasions exist where you can actually run into someone — the journey over, and the
village once you are there. A match has to be one of them.

```
same ride + corral    travelling together and penned together
same ride + wave      travelling together, same place and time once there
same corral
same wave             same village AND same wave
same ride             same vehicle at the same minute
```

First match wins, so each person gets exactly one reason. `sameRide` now **requires the
departure time** rather than treating it as a tiebreak.

**The one judgement call was wrong, and Sam corrected it the same day — see §23b.**

### Measured, not estimated

Ran both ladders over the 19-row imported roster, every runner's point of view:

| | directed matches |
|---|---|
| old | 130 |
| new | **22** |

The 83% that went: **70 `same village`, 34 `same ride`, 4 `same village + ride`** — the
three loose rungs and nothing else. What survived is 20 `same wave` and 2 `same corral`.
Zero `same ride` survived, because that roster predates the current form and only 3 of 19
gave a departure time, all different (§11). **Production should keep more of its ride
matches than this suggests** — §16 found 6 of 6 self-serve entries had one. Worth checking
after deploy:

```bash
npm run db:q:remote "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM v_runner_start WHERE transport_is_matchable=1 AND depart_time_local IS NOT NULL"
```

(I could not run this — production reads are blocked in the session sandbox.)

### An empty list is now a normal outcome

Three of nineteen end up with nobody near them, and that is the logic working. The section
used to vanish entirely when empty, which reads as the app having nothing to say. It now
explains itself, and says something different depending on whether you have given enough
information to be matched at all — no colour and wave, or no departure time, and the
honest answer is "fill this in", not "nobody matches you".

### A bug carried over from §14

`sameRide` checked **only my own** `transport_is_matchable`, never theirs. Not reachable
with real data — a shared `transport_key` means a shared `dim_transport` row and therefore
the same flag — but the rest of that file earns its correctness by never assuming exactly
this kind of thing. Fixed, and the reasoning is in the comment so nobody "simplifies" it
back.

### Verified

Five rungs and seven rejection cases exercised against the shipped ladder itself (pulled
out of `browse.js` rather than retyped, so the test cannot drift from the code): both-null
corrals, an unmatchable ride at a shared time, a shared ferry two hours apart, same wave
different village, same village different wave. Both empty-state branches checked in the
browser by moving the local fixture row to an unshared start and then clearing it, and the
fixture was restored afterwards.

### Still true

The §14 reasoning holds: overlap stays client-side because the browser already has the
roster and knows who you are, and each match is a real runner object so it can be starred
where you read it. §20's privacy model is the thing that would force this to the server —
you cannot withhold a field from the client and still match on it there.


### 23b. The village requirement, reversed — same day

> **Sam:** "I think it's ok if they're not in the same village, because they're walkable.
> I visited some friends in a different colour village from me on race morning last year."

Firsthand, and it beats the reasoning above — I had the three villages mentally sealed off
from each other. They are walkable.

**This is consistent with the rung that was cut, not a retreat from it.** What makes two
people findable is being there at the same *time*. The colour-only rung that went spanned
different waves and could be two hours apart. A shared wave across colours cannot be apart
at all: it is the same half-hour in the same venue, one walk away. Weaker than sharing a
village, not false.

So `sameWave` drops the colour, and a new rung keeps the distinction rather than
flattening it:

```
same ride + corral
same ride + wave
same corral
same village + wave    same place, same time, no walk
same ride
same wave              same time, one village away
```

A shared village still outranks a shared ride — the village is where you stand around for
half an hour, the ride is where you are herded.

**`sameCorral` deliberately keeps the colour, and that is load-bearing.** Corral letters
only mean something inside a colour: Orange C and Blue C are different pens in different
villages. Matching on the letter alone would send two people to opposite ends of Fort
Wadsworth to look for each other. There is a test for exactly this case, because it is the
obvious thing to "simplify" later.

**Directed matches on the 19-row roster, all three ladders:**

| | matches | nobody near them |
|---|---|---|
| original (before today) | 130 | 0 |
| village required (`998dd36`) | 22 | 3 |
| **walkable villages (`90fd499`)** | **52** | **1** |

Now: 30 `same wave`, 20 `same village + wave`, 2 `same corral`. The one person left with
nobody has no start info at all, so he gets the "fill this in" message rather than a bare
empty list.

**The pattern from §21 held again.** Every genuine correction this project has had came
from Sam or a tester, not from my own testing — and this one came from having actually
been at Fort Wadsworth, which is not a thing that can be derived from the seed data.

## 24. Built for the size it is growing into — 2026-10-29

Sam expects 50–200 users, not 22 and not the 1000 §20 was written for. Three changes,
three commits: `68a1b16`, `3a916b3`, `7fe64cf`. **Not yet deployed.**

### Seeding 200 locally — the method worth reusing

181 synthetic runners shaped like **production**, not uniformly: 100% with a wave, 69%
with a matchable ride *and* a departure time, ferry-dominant transport, departure times
clustered 05:00–06:00. Keyed from `runner_key >= 1000` so cleanup is two DELETEs. Generator
is in the session scratchpad, which is gone — regenerate it rather than hunting for it, the
shape above is the part that matters.

Uniform random data would have been useless here: the whole finding depends on the roster
being lumpy in the same places production is lumpy.

### Change 1 — "people near you" is now walked, not applied (`68a1b16`)

At 200 the median person got **44 suggestions**, one got **7,268px of them** — about ten
phone screens before reaching "Everyone". A second roster, not a shortlist.

The cause is density, not the ladder. Bare `same wave` is **58%** of matches at 200 and
**64%** at 22: the rung that rescues a thin roster drowns a full one.

So: take the strongest rung, then the next, stop once you have six. A crowded wave never
gets past its strong rungs; a lonely one keeps descending. Same code, different behaviour
by density.

**The obvious version of this is a trap, and measuring both sizes is the only thing that
catches it.** "Fall back to the weak rungs only if you have NO strong ones" sounds right.
On the real 22-person roster most people *do* have one strong match, so the weak rungs get
suppressed and the median person drops from **5 matches to 2** — it would have made the
live app worse on race day to fix a problem that does not exist until 200. Counting to six
instead of to one is a no-op at 22.

| | 200 seeded | 22 production |
|---|---|---|
| before | med 44, max 63 | med 5, max 6 |
| after | **med 13, max 20** | **med 5, max 6** |

Ceiling of 20 drawn, because the rung that crosses the target is taken whole — cutting a
category off mid-way is arbitrary. Five of 200 hit it; none of 22 do.

### Change 2 — filtering without rebuilding (`3a916b3`)

§21 expected `render()` to bite at 1000. **It bites at 200:** 111–178ms per keystroke on a
*Mac*, rebuilding 256 cards and 5,739 nodes on every keystroke. The target is a cold phone at 5am,
several times slower again.

Everyone's cards are built once and shown or hidden in place; the list is rebuilt only when
the data changes, never when the filter does.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| steady keystroke | 111–178ms | **0.3–3.7ms** |
| worst case | 178ms | **5.8ms** |

The worst case is now re-showing 100+ cards after a backspace, which is the right thing to
be bounded by.

The refocus-and-restore-caret dance is **gone, not reimplemented** — it only ever existed
to paper over the rebuild destroying the box being typed into.

**A real bug fell out of it.** `data-v` has to round-trip back to the value, and `esc(null)`
is `""`, which reads back as the empty string. The "All" chip is the only null, and it
silently lost its pressed state after being clicked — state used to be baked in at build
time, so nothing ever read it back. Now it round-trips.

`[hidden]` is `!important` in `app.css`: the UA sheet already says `display:none`, but any
later `display` rule on `.card` would outrank it and filtering would quietly stop hiding
anything.

### Change 3 — rate limiting (`7fe64cf`)

Closes the §16/§21 item. **I expected to use the Workers rate limiting binding and could
not: Pages Functions support only a subset of Workers bindings and `ratelimits` is not
among them** (KV, Durable Objects, R2, D1, Vectorize, Workers AI, service bindings, queues,
Hyperdrive, Analytics Engine, vars, secrets — that is the list).

That is the better outcome. The binding's `period` may only be **10 or 60 seconds**, so the
tightest it expresses is ~10/minute — still 17 hours to exhaust a 4-digit PIN — and its
counts are approximate and **per-Cloudflare-location**. D1 gives our own window, strongly
consistent, and it lives in the repo, which was the whole reason for preferring config over
a dashboard rule (§17).

```
signin    8 failures / 15 min, keyed on the TARGET bib-or-name
group    20 failures / 15 min, keyed on client IP
```

**Keying signin on the target rather than the caller is the deliberate part.** An attacker
rotates IPs freely but cannot change whose PIN they are attacking. And on race morning
thousands of people at Fort Wadsworth sit behind a handful of carrier-NAT addresses, where
an IP-keyed lockout would jam legitimate sign-ins at the worst possible moment. At 8 per 15
minutes a 4-digit PIN takes ~13 days; the app does not live that long.

Failures only; a correct answer clears the counter. A locked key is refused even with the
right secret, or it is not a lockout.

Verified against local D1: group allows 20 then 429s and refuses the correct passcode; a
target locks after 8 while another person is unaffected; keys are lowercased so `BRITNEY`
and `britney` share a budget; an aged window **resets in place** (8 → 1) rather than locking
someone out forever; success deletes the row; the prune sweeps stale keys.

### Deploying this — order matters

```bash
npm run db:migrate:remote     # 0006 FIRST
npm run deploy                # then the code
```

The other way round, every sign-in hits a missing table and 500s.

### Still not done

- ~~The six-digit PIN rule~~ — **DONE, `bce6862`. See §24b.**
- Dropping `bib_number` from the roster display (§21). Still the other half of the PIN
  attack, since the bib is the lookup key.
- §20's mutual-star model stays **overkill at 200** and would break the discovery loop the
  app exists for. Revisit only if it genuinely approaches 1000.


### 24b. Six-digit PINs — `bce6862`

The rule was four-to-six digits, and almost everyone picks the shortest thing a form
allows. Four digits is 10,000 combinations; six is 1,000,000 — a hundredfold for one
keystroke, which is why this was the cheapest win left.

Paired with the signin throttle from §24, at ~770 guesses a day, a full sweep goes from
roughly **thirteen days to about three and a half years**. The app lives three weeks.

**Nobody is locked out, and that is the load-bearing detail.** `signin.ts` never calls
`pinLooksValid` — it goes straight to `pinMatches` — so every existing four-digit PIN keeps
working. This binds PIN *creation* only, which is the growing half of the roster. Anyone
whose PIN is reset (§16) picks a six-digit one on the way back in. Verified end to end by
computing a real PBKDF2-10k hash of a four-digit PIN outside the app, planting it, and
signing in: **200**.

**Also added, and it is what makes the million real:** a weak-pattern check. 123456 and
111111 are perennially the two most common PINs in every breach corpus, and at 770 guesses
a day a *throttled* attacker still reaches them within minutes — so without this the
hundredfold is nominal. Rules rather than a word list: one repeated digit, a run of ±1, or
a two- or three-digit block repeated (121212, 123123). Measured by brute-forcing the whole
space: **1,100 of 1,000,000 blocked, 0.11%**, so the cost to anyone choosing honestly is
nil. `890123` is allowed, because it wraps and is not a clean run.

**One rule, one place.** The length is mirrored in `form.js` to catch it before a round
trip, as it already was. The "too obvious" half is server-side only, so the interesting
logic has one copy — the forms all surface whatever the server says, and the hint names
123456 so it is not a surprise.

Five places had to move together, which is the thing to check if this is ever touched
again: `lib/pin.ts` (the rule), `claim.ts` and `onboard.ts` (the messages, now shared
constants), and `form.js` (hint text **and** its own regex). `gate.js`'s sign-in field is
the one that must **not** change — it has no length rule by design, and adding one would
lock out every existing four-digit PIN.

### Deploy, in this order

```bash
npm run db:migrate:remote     # 0006 FIRST — §24
npm run deploy                # then all of §24 and §24b together
```

## 25. The teardown snapshot — 2026-10-29, `b74f968`

§8 said teardown was `d1 export` straight into `git add snapshots/`, and `db:snapshot` in
`package.json` *was* that command — one `npm run` away. The failure mode is not malice, it
is being tired at 11pm on race night and running the thing that is already there.

### What that command would have committed

| table | what it holds |
|---|---|
| `dim_runner` | `pin_hash` + `pin_salt` for every claimed runner |
| `fct_runner_start` | bib numbers, and every assignment *version* (insert-only) |
| `fct_runner_saved` | who starred whom — a social graph |
| `auth_throttle` | **client IP addresses** — new in `7fe64cf`, unanticipated by §8 |
| `d1_migrations` | wrangler bookkeeping, no analytical value |

Production also had **24 `dim_runner` rows against 22 on the live roster**: two people took
themselves off and are still fully present with their history. The UI does disclose that
("Removing you keeps your history in the snapshot"), so it is not a surprise sprung on
anyone — but opted-out people would be in the committed file.

### The argument, which the repo was already making

`.gitignore`, in its own words: the roster CSV is out of git because *"a name + bib is
enough to look someone up on NYRR tracking."* Then §8 planned to commit the same names and
bibs back in, with password hashes attached. **The input was treated as sensitive and the
output was not.** That is the whole issue in one sentence.

Git is also the wrong place to change your mind: commit now, delete in six months, still in
history — and §8 explicitly wants this file to be long-lived.

### The reframe that makes it cheap

What the snapshot is *for* is the dimensional model and the shape of the data — a real
factless fact table with real lumpy distributions, loadable into SQLite, DuckDB or Postgres
with no Cloudflare account. **None of that needs anybody's identity.** So nearly all of the
exposure goes while keeping all of the value.

```bash
npm run db:snapshot        # selected tables, PIN hashes always scrubbed
npm run db:snapshot:anon   # + synthetic names and bibs, distributions intact
```

### Three properties worth keeping

- **Scrubbing is SQL against a real SQLite database**, not a rewrite of the dump text.
  Names contain apostrophes, and a regex over `INSERT` statements works right up until the
  row where it does not. Proven with a name containing `'`, `"`, `;`, a `DROP TABLE` and a
  `--` comment: byte-intact round trip, all tables still standing.
- **It fails closed.** A table or column the script has not been told about aborts the run
  rather than being published — exactly the `auth_throttle` gap, which existed because the
  table was invented after §8 was written. The check earned itself on its first run by
  catching `_cf_METADATA`, which exists locally but not in production.
- **It verifies against the text that will actually be committed**: no dropped table
  defined or populated, no surviving hash, and under `--anonymise` no original name or bib
  anywhere in the file. A scrub that silently did nothing is the entire risk.

**Views are pulled from the live database and appended deliberately.** `--table` selects
tables only, and §8's revival path loads this file straight into a fresh D1 — the app reads
nothing but views, so a snapshot without them restores a database the app cannot use.
Verified: reloads into plain `sqlite3` with all 9 views and they query correctly.

### Still a decision, not automated away

Whether to use `--anonymise` is Sam's call and scales with roster size. At 22 friends the
real names are a keepsake. The script defaults to keeping them and prints a warning saying
so; it does not decide for you.

## 26. Roster cap and the outfit field — 2026-10-29, `b6bd988` + `fcb36bb`

Both answer questions Sam raised about growing to 50–200. **Not yet deployed.**

### Roster cap (`b6bd988`)

Measured at 200 seeded runners, 375px phone: the unfiltered Everyone list is **25,916px,
about forty screens**, and the whole page is 42.9. Draws 25 by default with a toggle;
page drops to **7.9 screens**.

**The cap is for undirected browsing only.** Any filter or search draws the whole matching
set — you have already said what you are looking for, and trimming the answer to a question
you asked is a different and worse thing than trimming a list you were idly scrolling.
Verified: a wave filter shows all 40 and the button disappears.

**Not keyed to viewport**, despite that being the obvious reading of Sam's question. The
layout is `max-width: 620px` and the badge row fits without wrapping at 313px, so a card is
the same height everywhere — measured **identical (2552px for 20 cards) at 343, 620 and
768px**. A viewport-dependent cap adds a variable that changes nothing visible.

**Not pagination, not tabs.** Tabs would duplicate the colour/wave/transport filters that
already exist. Pagination on a browse list costs taps, loses your place and breaks
find-in-page.

Two details worth keeping:

- `matched` and `drawn` are tracked separately, so the heading reads "Everyone (199)" when
  nothing is filtered rather than "Everyone (25 of 199)" — the latter looks like the app
  hid something you asked for. The live region carries the truncation instead.
- The control is a **toggle**, not a button that vanishes, so expanding never destroys the
  element holding focus.

**Dormant at the current size** (18 others, under the cap). Same property as the adaptive
ladder: no change today, fixes 200.

### The outfit field (`fcb36bb`)

The field that actually finds somebody at Fort Wadsworth was called **"Note"**, hinted
"what to look for", placeheld "orange poncho, by the Starbucks". It was already the outfit
field and never said so, and a box labelled "Note" gets skipped.

Now *"What you'll be wearing · optional — throwaway layers too"*. **Throwaway layers are
the point** and the thing nobody mentions: it is dark and cold, everyone is in an old
hoodie, and the singlet you would describe is underneath it where nobody can see it.

Label, hint and placeholder only — same column, same 140 chars, existing entries untouched.
The validation message follows ("outfit note"), and `.note` is no longer `--muted` on the
card: it is the line that identifies a person in the dark, and it was in the colour
reserved for things you can skip — the same mistake the start line made before §22.

### Photos — researched, deliberately not built

**Feasible.** R2 bucket bindings *are* supported on Pages Functions, free tier is 10 GB /
1M Class A / 10M Class B with free egress. 200 users × 3 images client-resized to ~150KB is
**~90 MB, under 1% of the allowance**.

**Not built, and timing is the decisive reason** — three days to race day for ~250–350
lines whose failure modes are privacy failures, on a live app. What would bite, in order:

1. **EXIF GPS.** Phone photos carry coordinates; someone photographs their outfit at home
   and publishes their address. A client-side canvas re-encode strips it and you want that
   for resizing anyway — but you have to know.
2. **It changes what the app is**: name + face + bib + where they'll be + when. A bib is
   revocable; a face is not.
3. **No moderation path**, and at 200 friends-of-friends the social cost of misbehaving
   stops being a deterrent.
4. **A second teardown surface** that §25's work does not cover — "app is gone, bucket
   still holds everyone's faces".
5. **R2 has no hard spending cap.** Above free tier it bills and stays up.

Also weaker than it looks as a product: a photo of a race kit is a photo of something
hidden under a throwaway layer in the dark. **Good 2027 feature with time to do properly.**

## 27. Instagram handles, bib canonicalisation, and the shared link — 2026-10-29

Three commits, all **undeployed**: `df0bd25`, `5f2b668`, `4f76d2a` (plus stamp `99808cb`).
Deploy needs **migration 0007 first**.

### Bib collisions — audited, two holes closed (`df0bd25`)

Sam asked whether a bib already taken is handled when someone new types it. Tested against
local D1:

| input | before |
|---|---|
| `9xxxx` when taken | 409, *"already on the roster — are you already in here?"* |
| editing onto a taken bib | 409, *"...already on the roster for someone else"* |
| `"  9xxxx  "` | 409 — trimmed, collides correctly |
| `9xxxx` | **201 CREATED** — hole |
| `not-a-bib` | **201 CREATED** — hole |

The live-bib unique index compares **raw strings**, so `9xxxx` and `9xxxx` were two bibs to
the database and one bib to a human. Leading zeros are now stripped before the index sees
them, and bibs must be digits. All 29 production bibs are four or five digits with no
leading zero, so nothing existing is invalidated.

Both matter more now: behind a passcode a bad bib is a typo between friends; on an open
sign-up it is how one person ends up holding a number belonging to someone who has not
joined yet. **Sam will handle squatting by hand** — not worth building for 150–300 people.

### Instagram handle (`5f2b668`)

The cheap half of §26's photo question: no uploads, no R2, no EXIF, no moderation, no second
teardown surface. On `dim_runner`, because a handle is an attribute of the **person** and
does not change when they move wave — where `meetup_note` is about this race's meetup and
correctly sits on the fact. `display_name` is already UPDATEd on edit, so it follows a path
that exists.

Normalises whatever people paste: `@handle`, a full profile URL, a tracking query string,
mixed-case host. `v_runner_start` is rebuilt (SQLite has no ALTER VIEW) — **all seven
dependent views verified still returning rows** afterwards.

Two things testing caught that reading would not have:

- The card pill is **the first pill that is a tap target**, and measured **23px** — under
  §19's 24px floor for 2.5.8. Given its own padding; the others are text and resizing them
  would reflow the badge rows.
- A silent no-op: the handle validated but stored as `null`, because a replacement did not
  match and I had not asserted on that one edit. Caught by querying the database instead of
  trusting the 201. **Assert on every scripted edit.**

The icon is a plain camera, not the Instagram mark, which is a brand asset.

**The exposure note that matters:** a handle is a far stronger identifier than a bib. A bib
expires with the race; a handle is a durable link to a real social identity, sitting beside
where somebody will physically be and when. Fine behind the passcode. It is the single most
exposing column in the database the moment the passcode comes off.

### The shared link (`4f76d2a`)

`https://nycm26friendfinder.com/?k=<password>` — one thing to paste instead of a link plus
a password people then lose. Redeemed before anything renders, then **stripped with
`history.replaceState`**, so the address bar, screenshots, bookmarks, the back button and
any outbound `Referer` stay clean. A dead key is stripped too and falls back to the form.

**Framed honestly: "unlisted, not private."** Once the link is in a few group chats the
password is not a secret — it is forwarded and screenshotted. It stops crawlers, scrapers
and anyone who just types the domain. It does not stop anyone who was sent it. Right size
of boundary for a running club, wrong one for the open internet.

**The escape hatch, and it is better than expected:** group tokens are HMAC'd with
`TOKEN_SECRET`, **not** with the password. So

```bash
npx wrangler pages secret put GROUP_PASSCODE --project-name nycm-friendfinder
```

kills every old link **without signing out a single person already in**. Rotate and
re-share if it spreads too far. (Unlike `TOKEN_SECRET`, which §16 says never to rotate —
that one does sign everyone out.)

Companions: `robots.txt` + `noindex` on both pages (a crawler already gets only an empty
shell, so this is about not surfacing in search at all), and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`
on `/` and `/me`, now the only pages linking off-site.

### Deploy order

```bash
npm run db:migrate:remote     # 0007 FIRST — the roster view gains a column
npm run deploy
```

Reversed, every roster read hits a view without `instagram`.

### Not done, deliberately

Removing the password entirely. That is the §20 trigger, and it interacts badly with
handles: a public roster plus Instagram handles is a public directory linking real social
identities to where ~200 people will be and when. The shared link gets the sharing
ergonomics without crossing that line.
