## 29. The header, and where to pick up — current resume point, 2026-10-29

**This section supersedes §28 as the resume point.** §28 stays accurate for everything it
describes; it just no longer ends the story. §16 is still the production reference.

### What changed

The header was a 17px title sharing a flex row with "Edit my info". For a link people tap
out of a group chat that read like a utility page, so it now has a Futura wordmark and a
drawn mark of two runners mid-stride.

| | commit |
|---|---|
| Header wordmark + runner mark | `c9c6e68` |
| Build stamp | `0e331ea` |

Live and verified. Build `9dd1d0150e1c`.

**The header is two rows now** — brand on its own line, date and link sharing the line
below. That is forced, not stylistic: the wordmark wants 274px at full size and a 390px
phone has 358px of content width. The two could not share a row at display size.

**No webfont, deliberately.** Futura on macOS/iOS, Avenir Next → Century Gothic → system-ui
elsewhere. A downloaded font is either a blocking request or a visible swap, and this gets
read at Fort Wadsworth at 5am with fifty thousand people on one cell tower. Nothing in the
header waits on the network. Only the h1 uses it.

**The mark is drawn, not borrowed** — same rule as the camera in §27, same 24-unit grid and
round caps as the PATHS map in `app.js`, so it sits in the same hand as the transport
icons. The companion runner is `--muted` rather than the same stroke at reduced opacity: a
transparency multiplies against whatever is behind it and stops being a measured value,
and `--muted` already is one in both themes. `aria-hidden`; the h1 still carries the name.

**Sizing.** `clamp(21px, 0.2rem + 5.7vw, 26px)`, set on `.brand` rather than the h1 so the
mark can be sized in `em` and the block grows as one unit. Sizing the mark in px let the
wordmark outgrow it on a wide screen and crowd it on a narrow one.

The middle term keeps a `rem` in it **on purpose**. A size in `vw` alone does not grow when
somebody raises their default font size — the viewport shrinks in CSS px by the same factor
everything is magnified — so a pure-`vw` title quietly fails 1.4.4 while looking fine. The
rem term is the one that responds. Measured, not eyeballed:

| viewport | size | title vs content width | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 320px | 21.4px | 226 of 288 | one line |
| 360px | 23.7px | 250 of 328 | one line |
| 390px | 25.4px | 268 of 358 | one line |
| 430px | 26.0px | 274 of 398 | one line |

No horizontal overflow at any width. At a doubled default font size it reflows to two lines
and still does not overflow — content reflows, nothing is clipped. That is the correct
1.4.4 outcome.

§19 kept intact: heading order, the 5px vertical padding holding the header link at the
24px target floor, `#edit-link`'s id and `hidden` (browse.js still finds it and swaps the
text to "Add me back"), and the live region outside `#app`.

`me.html` takes the type but not the mark — the runners belong beside the name they
illustrate, and "My info" is a sub-page, not the brand.

### Known limitation, not a bug

**320px leaves 13px of slack, and that figure is for Futura.** On a device without it the
fallback is wider and the title wraps to two lines. It wraps rather than clipping, so it
degrades correctly, but a first-generation iPhone SE or an Android phone will not match the
screenshots. If somebody sends a screenshot that looks wrong, this is why — check the
device before changing the clamp.

### A new way the tooling lies

**`curl -I` on `/api/*` reports the wrong cache headers.** `curl -I /api/meta` comes back
`public, max-age=0, must-revalidate` and looks exactly like `no-store` has regressed. It
has not: **Pages does not route HEAD to the Function** and answers it itself. `GET` returns
`no-store` correctly.

Check API cache headers with `curl -s -D - -o /dev/null`, never with `-I`.

This is the same shape of lie as §17's splat: the thing you naturally reach for reports
something plausible while telling you nothing about the real path. §17 was `wrangler pages
dev` parsing `_headers` rules production ignores; this is `-I` probing a path the Function
never sees. **Both were caught only by checking the live GET.** That is now two independent
instances of the same trap, which makes it a rule rather than an anecdote.

### Git state — read this before assuming anything is backed up

**`origin` was 24 commits behind and had been since before §17.** Everything from
`534f1fd` ("Stop the browser holding the app's modules for four hours") through §27's
shared-link work existed only on this machine. Pushing `0e331ea` fast-forwarded all of it
in one go. `main` and `origin/main` are now level.

Checked at the same time, because pushing that much at once is when it matters:

- **The repo is PRIVATE.** Confirmed via `gh repo view`, not assumed.
- **No real roster data is tracked.** `.gitignore` excludes `*.csv` and `seed/` with the
  reason written next to it — a name plus a bib is enough to look somebody up on NYRR
  tracking. `snapshots/` holds only `.gitkeep`. `.dev.vars` is ignored.
- `project_notes.md` — this file — is gitignored and **has never been pushed**. It is on
  this machine only. If the machine dies, these notes die with it.

Nothing was exposed by the push. But the lesson is that "committed" had meant "on one
laptop" for about two weeks, and nobody noticed because the deploys were going out fine.
**`wrangler pages deploy` does not touch git.** A clean `git status` says nothing about
whether `origin` has any of it.

### Still open, carried forward from §28

All four of §28's open items stand unchanged: **bib squatting** (handled by hand, surfaces
as a 409), **removing the password** (deliberately not done — it is the §20 trigger and
interacts badly with Instagram handles), **photos** (declined for 2026, good 2027 feature),
and **`--anonymise` on the final snapshot** (decide at teardown; it matters if this repo
ever goes public or into a portfolio — note that it is private today, so that decision has
not been forced).

The teardown sequence in §28 is unchanged and still correct.

### The pattern, again

§28 said every genuine correction came from Sam or a tester rather than my own testing.
This section is another: the runners were drawn upright and competent-looking until Sam
said "more in a running motion, like mid-stride" and attached two references. The pose was
the whole point of the mark and I had quietly settled for the easy version of it.

The other half is that **three of the four things worth writing down here were found by
measuring rather than looking** — the clamp arithmetic, the 320px slack, and the `-I`
trap. The header looked right in a screenshot in all three cases.

### Priority order and why

| 1 | "what is this / why" screen | high | low | **yes** |
| 2 | filters behind a disclosure | medium | medium | probably |
| 4 | spectator mode + pace projection | high | **high — schema change** | **skeleton only; decide separately** |

§29 measured the thing that makes 1 and 3 urgent: **423 unique visitors, 36 signups,
8.5%.** `/api/runners` is `requireProfile`, so ~390 people were asked to create a PIN
before being shown a single reason to. 1 and 3 both attack that number. 2 and 4 do not.

---

### 3. The shared link loses its password — ROOT CAUSE FOUND

Not a typo in the URL. `gate.js redeemLinkKey()` strips `?k=` with
`history.replaceState` the instant the page loads — deliberately, per §27, so a
screenshot or a Referer cannot carry the password onward.

**The consequence nobody drew out: forwarding from the address bar loses the password.**

```
Alice opens  …/?k=SECRET   -> address bar becomes  …/   (stripped, by design)
Alice taps Share / copies the URL -> sends  …/  with no key
Bob lands on "Group password" and has to ask Sam
```

That is exactly the reported symptom. The security feature and the sharing feature are
in direct conflict, and sharing lost. iOS Share Sheet, "Copy Link" in Safari, and
copy-pasting the address bar all reproduce it.

**A second, independent defect in the same function.** `redeemLinkKey` wraps `/api/auth`
in `try {} catch {}` and strips the key *whatever* went wrong. A wrong key should strip
(§27, correct). **A network blip, a 5xx or a 429 should not** — the key is destroyed, the
refresh does not retry, and the only recovery is finding the original link again. A
transient failure permanently burns that tap.

**Fix, two parts, both additive:**

1. **`GET /api/invite`** — returns the full `…/?k=<passcode>` URL. Gated on a valid group
   token, so only somebody already inside can mint one. The server already holds
   `GROUP_PASSCODE`; this keeps the passcode out of `localStorage` entirely, which a
   client-side "remember the key" fix would not.
2. **A "Copy invite link" control** in the UI that calls it. Makes forwarding the *right*
   link the easy path, which is the only durable fix for a human behaviour.
3. **Distinguish 401 from transient.** Strip on 401 (dead key, §27 stands). Keep the key
   in the URL on network error / 429 / 5xx so a refresh retries.

**Testing (this is the part Sam asked to be extensive):** a harness that exercises
redeem + strip + forward across the real failure modes, run against the live domain and
a local server. Enumerated in §31.

---

### 1. "What is this and why" screen

Placement: after the password gate, **before** "Who are you?". Sam's own words from his
post, trimmed for a phone screen, tone preserved. Must not become a wall — a short
headline, 3-4 beats, then straight into the existing buttons.

Open question for Sam: **one screen with the buttons on it, or a screen you dismiss?**
Default assumption unless told otherwise: **same screen** — copy on top, buttons below.
One less tap, and it cannot be skipped accidentally.

Accessibility: h2 stays the heading, copy is prose, buttons keep the existing markup
from `askWhoYouAre`. No new interactive patterns, so §19 is untouched.

---

### 2. Filters behind a disclosure

Today `filterBar()` draws three always-on rows of chips — colour, wave, transport — which
is ~5 rows of vertical space before a single person is visible. Sam's screenshot is
mostly filter.

**Keep the chips, hide them behind a disclosure.** A `<button aria-expanded>` labelled
"Filter" with a count of what is active, opening a panel containing the groups exactly as
they are now.

**Why not `<select multiple>`,** which is the literal reading of the request: native
multi-selects are genuinely bad on iOS, and converting would throw away the `aria-pressed`
/ `role="group"` / labelled-group work §19 did. A disclosure wrapping the existing chips
is the same interaction Sam described ("a menu that opens to multi-select buttons") at a
fraction of the risk.

**Behaviour change, deliberate: single-select -> multi-select.** `filter.color` and friends
are scalars today (`matches()` does `r.color_name === filter.color`). Going to Sets means
"Orange OR Pink". Within a dimension: OR. Across dimensions: AND.

---

### 4. Spectator mode + goal time + mile projections

Prompted by Kat C ("what if I am here to spectate"), Runner E and Runner I
(multiple miles; sign/cowbell; handing out support). Today the advice is "fill it out
without a bib", which puts a spectator on the roster as a blank card that matches nobody
— exactly the three dead profiles §29 found.

**Skeleton scope, in dependency order:**

1. **Migration 0008.**
   - `fct_runner_start.participant_role TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'runner'`
     `CHECK (participant_role IN ('runner','spectator'))`. On the fact, not the dim:
     spectating is about *this race*, same reasoning §27 used for `meetup_note` vs
     `instagram`.
   - `fct_runner_start.goal_time_seconds INTEGER` — runner's goal finish.
   - `fct_spectator_mile (runner_start_key, mile_marker)` — a table, not a column,
     because Runner I explicitly asked for several.
   - `has_sign`, `has_support` INTEGER flags.
   - Rebuild `v_runner_start` (SQLite has no ALTER VIEW — §27 hit this).
2. **Projection, pure function, no storage.** `elapsed(mile) = goal * mile / 26.2`;
   `clock(mile) = wave start_time_local + elapsed`. Linear on purpose for the skeleton —
   NYC's profile is not linear and the bridges are slow, but a wrong-but-honest even
   split beats a fake-precise model, and the label must say "estimate".
3. **Matching.** Spectators must not fall through the runner ladder. A spectator matches
   on *mile overlap* with other spectators, and "following" a runner is the existing
   `fct_runner_saved` table — it already exists and already has the right shape.
4. **UI.** Role picker at onboarding; mile multi-select for spectators; goal-time field
   for runners; a projected-splits table on a followed runner.

**This is the one with real risk.** It changes the schema, the view every page reads, and
the semantics of the roster, roughly 30 hours before 56 people depend on it working.
**Default plan: build and test it fully, deploy it only on Sam's explicit say-so,**
separately from 1/2/3.

### 3. The link — root cause and fix

Cause confirmed, written up in §30: `gate.js` strips `?k=` on arrival (§27, correct), so
**forwarding from the address bar forwards a link with no password**. Everybody who said
"it asked me for a password" had been sent a stripped URL by somebody already inside.

Shipped three things:

- **`GET /api/invite`** returns `…/?k=<passcode>`, gated on a valid group token, built from
  the request's own origin so it is right on the custom domain, `.pages.dev` and locally.
  The passcode stays server-side — a "remember the key in localStorage" fix would have put
  it on every device, which is the posture §27 deliberately avoided.
- **A "Copy invite link" control** on the roster, with the reason written next to it.
  Falls back to showing the link in a selectable field when `navigator.clipboard` refuses,
  which iOS does often enough that a silent failure would be the worst possible outcome
  for the one control whose entire job is fixing sharing.
- **A second defect in the same function, fixed.** `redeemLinkKey` caught *everything* and
  stripped the key regardless, so a dropped connection, a 429 or a 5xx destroyed a good
  link and the refresh had nothing left to retry with. Now only a 401 strips.

**`test_link.sh`, 18 assertions, all green**: auth 200/401, invite 200 with a token and 401
without one and 401 on a forged one, `no-store` on the invite response, the minted key
round-trips back to a token, and `gate.js` only strips on 401.

Section 4 of that suite checks the passcode is URL-safe — no `#` (truncates at the
fragment), `&`, space, `+` or non-ascii, and survives an encode/decode round trip. **All
pass, which rules out chat-app mangling** and leaves forwarding as the whole story.
Caveat: that ran against the LOCAL passcode. Re-run it against production after deploying
and check the shape of what `/api/invite` returns without printing it.

### 1. The "why"

Sam's own words, trimmed to a phone screen, placed in `askWhoYouAre` **above** the buttons
— the exact screen §29 measured ~390 people bouncing off. `h2.lede` overrides the small
uppercase section-label style back to a sentence; still an h2, so the h1 → h2 order §19
verified is untouched. Body copy is full `--text`, not `--muted`, for the same reason the
outfit line is (§26): muted is the colour for things you can skip.

### 2. Filters

Collapsed behind a `Filter (n)` disclosure with a Clear button. The chips are **unchanged**
— same `aria-pressed`, same `role="group"`, now three labelled groups instead of two.
Deliberately not `<select multiple>`: bad on iOS, and it would have thrown away §19's work.

**Single-select → multi-select.** `filter.color/wave/transport` are Sets; OR within a
dimension, AND across. The null "All" chip clears its own dimension.

Verified in the browser: Orange 8, Orange∪Pink 12, ∩Wave 1 → 5, un-toggle Pink → 3, Clear
→ 18. Count badge tracked throughout. Re-checked §19: every chip keeps `aria-pressed`,
"All" is pressed only when its dimension is empty, `aria-controls` on the toggle, and the
live region still sits outside `#app` and still announces.

### 4. Spectators — what exists

**Migration 0008** (local only): `participant_role` and `goal_time_seconds` on
`fct_runner_start`, `has_sign` / `has_support` flags, and `fct_spectator_mile` as a TABLE
because Runner I asked for several miles. On the fact table, not the dim — spectating is
about this race, same call §27 made for `meetup_note`.

`is_complete` is now **per role**: a spectator with a mile is complete without a bib, a
wave or a corral. That is the fix for Runner E's workaround ("fill it out without a bib"),
which produced exactly the dead blank cards §29 found.

**Projection** (`projectSplits` in `app.js`) is deliberately even-paced. A real New York
split is nothing like linear — the Verrazzano, First Avenue, the Fifth Avenue climb at 23
— and modelling it needs per-runner data nobody has. Even pacing answers "mile 18 at 11:30
or 12:30?" to within a few minutes; a fitted curve would be wrong by about as much while
looking authoritative. **The caption says "estimate only" and must keep saying it.**
27 unit tests, all green, including clock-wrap for a wave-5 six-hour finisher.

**Goal times are followers-only**, per Sam. The subtlety that nearly shipped wrong:
`/api/runners` is `SELECT *` over `v_runner_start`, and the view has to carry the column
because `/me` reads through it to fill in your own edit form. So **the roster endpoint
strips it for everyone but the caller**, via an explicit `PRIVATE_TO_FOLLOWERS` list —
nulled rather than never-selected, so a future column added to the view cannot silently
widen that endpoint. Verified over the API: 0 other rows carry a goal; the follower path
through `v_saved_overlap` still does.

**A bug that only appeared on screen.** A complete spectator was still listed under "still
missing info", because `v_roster_gaps` asks `is_complete = 0 OR transport_key IS NULL` and
then names bib/colour/wave/corral as what is missing. For someone who will never have a
bib that is both wrong and discouraging — the precise tone problem spectators exist to
fix. `v_roster_gaps` is now role-aware and says "a mile". **It was not in my list of views
to rebuild**; the three obvious dependents were, and this one was found by reading the
rendered page. §27's "rebuild every dependent view" needs to mean all nine, not the three
that mention the column.

Because 0008 had never been deployed, the fix went INTO 0008 rather than a 0009, and the
local database was reset and **all eight migrations replayed from empty** — which also
proves 0008 applies to a fresh database, not just to this one.

### What is NOT done

- **Spectator-to-spectator matching.** A spectator currently falls through the runner
  ladder and matches nobody. §30 planned mile-overlap matching; it is not built. Two
  spectators at mile 18 will not find each other.
- **Following from the spectator side** reuses `fct_runner_saved` and works, but there is
  no "spectators near you" section.
- **`/api/invite` has no rate limit.** It needs a valid group token, so it is not an open
  oracle, but it will hand out the passcode as often as it is asked.
- A pre-existing raciness in `onboard.ts` — `SELECT runner_key … ORDER BY runner_key DESC
  LIMIT 1` to find the row it just created — is untouched. Two simultaneous signups could
  cross. Not introduced here, but the spectator miles now hang off that same key.

### Deploy order when Sam says go

1/2/3 carry no schema change and can go alone:
```bash
npm run deploy
```
4 needs the migration first, and it is one-way:
```bash
npx wrangler d1 migrations apply nycm-friendfinder --remote   # 0008
npm run deploy
```
**Apply the migration before the deploy, not after** — the new frontend reads columns the
old schema does not have. Then re-run `test_link.sh` against the live domain.

### Splitting the tree was the real work, and it was not optional

The four workstreams were interleaved across three files. Items 1/2/3 could not simply
be deployed from the working tree, because item 4's backend would have **broken
production immediately**: `onboard.ts` and `runners/me.ts` INSERT into
`participant_role`, `goal_time_seconds`, `has_sign`, `has_support` and
`fct_spectator_mile`, none of which exist at 0007. Every new signup and every profile
edit would have failed with a SQLite error.

`form.js` was the subtler hazard. Reverting only the backend would have left the role
picker on screen with no role-aware validation behind it, so anyone choosing
"I'm spectating" would have been written as a runner with no bib, no colour, no wave —
which is *precisely* the dead blank card §29 found three of. Shipping half of item 4
would have manufactured the bug item 4 exists to remove.

How it was done, in case this is ever needed again:
1. All 11 changed/new files copied to the scratchpad first. Nothing relied on git.
2. The six item-4-only files reverted with `git checkout --`.
3. `app.css` and `browse.js` stripped by script with **one assertion per edit** —
   each anchor had to match exactly once or the file was left untouched. 7 edits in
   `browse.js`, 1 in `app.css`, all verified.
4. Grepped the whole of `public/`, `functions/` and `lib/` for every item-4
   identifier. Zero hits before committing.
5. The branch was then rebuilt **from the committed base**, not from the snapshot, and
   the item-4 blocks re-applied by the inverse script — see the clipboard note below
   for why that mattered.

The local D1 had 0008 applied, so it was *not* production-shaped and would have hidden
exactly the class of bug being guarded against. `0008_spectators_and_goals.sql` was
moved out of `migrations/`, `npm run db:reset:local` replayed 0001–0007, and the seed
was reloaded — 19 runners on a database schema-identical to production. Confirmed the
0008 columns were absent from `fct_runner_start` before testing anything.

Also confirmed from the remote side: `wrangler d1 migrations list --remote` showed

Results on that database: typecheck clean, all modules parse, **21/21** shared-link
assertions, filter sequence measured in the page at 18 → 8 (Orange) → 12 (∪ Pink) →

`npm run db:migrate:local` to resume item 4.

### A real bug, found only because the deploy was verified in a browser

`navigator.clipboard.writeText` **never settled**. Not rejected — pending past three
seconds, with `document.hasFocus() === true` and `visibilityState === "visible"`.

The handler awaited it bare inside `try { … } catch {}`. A promise that never settles
is the one outcome that shape cannot survive: the `catch` never runs, the fallback
never runs, and the button stays `disabled` wearing its original label. Tap
"Copy invite link" → nothing happens, ever, until the page is reloaded. On the one
control whose entire purpose is to fix sharing, and whose own comment said a silent
failure would be the worst outcome.

Isolated it by racing the two awaits separately: `/api/invite` resolved in **10 ms**
with a valid `?k=`; the clipboard write was still pending at 3000 ms. Fixed with
`copyToClipboard()` — a 1200 ms race — and the button is now re-enabled on every
path. Re-tested in the same hostile condition: settles at 1474 ms, button re-enabled,
label "Copy this link:", live region announces honestly, fallback input appears with
the link pre-selected.

**WebKit is the reason to keep this even if Chrome stops doing it.** The gesture grant
is dropped across the `await` on the fetch that precedes the copy, so iOS — most of
this roster — is the likeliest place to land in the degraded path. The degraded path
now works.

This fix exists only on `main`, and it is why the branch was rebuilt from the
committed base: the scratchpad snapshot predates the fix, so restoring it wholesale
would have silently reverted the clipboard guard on `spectator-mode`. Verified by
diffing the branch against the snapshot — the only difference is the fix.

`/index.html` returns no `Cache-Control`. **Not a regression** — `_headers` is
exact-path (§17) and the canonical path is `/`, which does carry the rule.

### `wrangler pages deploy` reads the environment off the git branch

This is the trap of the session and it is worth writing down plainly.

Sam ran the three corrected commands, and the second and third both did something — but
not what the output implied. `wrangler d1 migrations apply --remote` applied 0008 to the
live database, and then `npm run deploy` **from `spectator-mode` published a Preview, not
Production**: Pages derives the environment from the current branch, `main` → Production
and anything else → Preview. The deploy said "✨ Deployment complete!" and gave a
`*.pages.dev` URL, exactly as it does for a production deploy.

So for about four minutes production was in a **split state**:

| | state |
|---|---|
| Database (shared, one D1) | 0008 — spectator columns, `fct_spectator_mile`, rebuilt views |
| Production code | `b4e9aaf95a4b` / `3eb5025` — items 1/2/3, no spectator code |
| Spectator code | live only at `863cd2d4.nycm-friendfinder.pages.dev` |

**Schema ahead of code is the safe direction** and nothing broke: the four new columns all
have defaults, so the old `onboard.ts` and `me.ts` kept inserting fine. Verified: 9 views,
63 runners, 59 current starts **all defaulted to `participant_role = 'runner'`**, 35
follows, 34 overlaps, zero data loss.

**But there was one real hole.** Production's `/api/runners` was still
`SELECT * FROM v_runner_start` with no `PRIVATE_TO_FOLLOWERS` strip — that code was part of
item 4 — while the rebuilt view now carried `goal_time_seconds`. Nothing leaked, because
no goal time existed yet. The vector was that **the preview build has the goal-time form
and writes to the same database**, so one person using that URL would have had their goal
time served to the whole roster, against Sam's explicit followers-only call. Closed by
finishing the deploy rather than by patching.

**There is no per-environment D1 binding.** `wrangler.toml` has one
`database_id = 146d5f13…`, so preview and production share the live database. A preview
deploy is not a safe sandbox for anything that writes.

## 34. PLAN — entry flow, invite placement, section dimensionality, 2026-10-30 ~12:40 ET

Sam's asks, in his order. Written before any code, per his standing instruction.

**Blocked: the filter restyle.** He attached three screenshots from macOS's
`NSIRD_screencaptureui_*` staging folder and the sandbox refuses it —
`Operation not permitted` from both the Read tool and `ls`. Asked him to paste them into
the chat or save them somewhere readable. Everything else below is fully specified in
words, so it proceeds now rather than waiting.

### 1. "Copy invite link" to the top, under the header, before the user's own card

Currently the last block before Sign out. Moving it means it is the first thing in
`#app`.

It must not become the loudest thing on the page — the person's own card should still be
what the eye lands on. So it goes in as a **compact bar**, not the current
heading + paragraph + button: one row with the button and a short hint, visually a strip
rather than a section.

Keeps `id="invite"`, so the click handler and the clipboard guard are untouched. The h2
becomes `sr-only` so heading navigation does not lose the landmark while the visual
weight drops.

### 2. Role before new/returning — two screens instead of one

Today: password → one screen with why + three buttons (claim / been here / new).

Sam wants: why passage → **I'm running / I'm spectating** → **I'm new / I've been here
before**, so the entrance points are distinct.

Wording: **"I'm running" / "I'm spectating"**, not "I'm racing". It matches the form's
existing chips exactly, and "racing" quietly excludes the charity and
first-timer-just-finishing crowd, who are a real part of this roster.

- `askWhoYouAre` splits into `askRole(root, next)` → `askNewOrReturning(root, next, role)`.
- The chosen role flows into onboarding as `entryFields(meta, { participant_role: role })`.
  No signature change — `entryFields` already derives its role chip state from
  `cur.participant_role`. The form still shows the picker, so the choice is visible and
  reversible rather than silently locked in.
- Back links both ways, so neither screen is a trap.

**Known wrinkle, deliberate:** for a returning person the role tap does nothing — their
stored profile already carries their role, and signin ignores it. Sam asked for this
order and it is defensible as framing rather than data entry, so it stays, but it is one
tap that buys a returning user nothing.

**Where "Someone already added me" goes.** Production has **0** claimable rows
(`v_unclaimed_runner`), because self-serve onboarding always sets a PIN — so that button
is already never rendered live. It stays conditional on `claimable > 0` and moves onto the
returning screen, which is where somebody already on the list would look. The two primary
entrances stay exactly two.

### 4. Dimensionality between sections

The page is a flat run of identical white cards on grey, separated only by an 11px muted
label. That is the "too cohesive" complaint: nothing says where "Your people" stops and
"People near you" starts.

Considered the full iOS inset-grouped-list treatment — drop the per-person borders and
make each *section* one rounded panel with hairline rows. It is the strongest version and
genuinely the researched answer for a 58-row list, but it rewrites every card on the page
(stars, pills, overlap tags, the splits table) two days before the race. Not worth that
risk now; noted as the 2027 move.

Shipping instead, which is the same idea at contained blast radius:
- Each block wrapped in `<section class="sec">`, with real spacing between sections and a
  hairline at each boundary — the delineation Sam named as the floor.
- A **section header band**: the h2 gets a solid background, a bottom hairline, and the
  count as a **pill** instead of parenthetical text, so it reads as a header belonging to
  its section rather than a label floating above it.
- **Sticky section headers.** This is the researched win and the reason not to stop at
  lines: on a 58-row list the header stays put while you scroll, so you always know
  whether you are in "People near you" or "Everyone". Standard iOS table-view behaviour,
  one `position: sticky` and no markup cost.

`applyFilter()` writes `#everyone-head.textContent`, which would wipe a child pill. So the
Everyone heading splits into a static label plus `#everyone-count`, and `applyFilter`
writes the count only.

## 35. Spectators don't travel to the start — built, NOT deployed, 2026-10-30 ~13:05 ET

Sam, after looking at the live spectator form: spectators will not be "getting to the
start line" or have a departure time, and the mile buttons do not fit the page. Plus a
question — what would it take for spectators to see who is near them.

**Still cannot read his screenshots.** Fourth one, same `NSIRD_screencaptureui_*` staging
folder, same `EPERM` from both the Read tool and `ls`. The filter restyle from §34 is
still outstanding and so is whatever this one showed; everything below came from his
written description.

### Transport is a runner question

Every row of `dim_transport` is a way to reach the Staten Island start — the ferry, the
Verrazzano buses, the charity coaches. 0008 said "transport stays a gap for both, because
everybody has to get there", which is true of getting somewhere and false of getting to
the start. Somebody watching at mile 18 in Manhattan takes none of them.

Three places had to agree:
- `form.js` — transport and departure wrapped in `#f-getting-there` and added to
  `paintRole`'s hide list, so a spectator is never shown them.
- `validate.ts` — nulls `transport_key` and `depart_time_local` for spectators. Needed
  because somebody can fill the runner half in, switch role and submit.
- `migrations/0009` — rebuilds `v_roster_gaps` so transport is not a gap for a spectator,
  **and fixes the WHERE clause**, which ORed in `transport_key IS NULL` and would have
  dragged back every spectator the CASE had just stopped describing. Also clears transport
  from any existing spectator row.

Verified on a local DB replayed from empty through all 9 migrations: a spectator with
mile 18 and no transport is `is_complete = 1` and **not** in `v_roster_gaps`; a spectator
with no mile is listed as missing `a mile` and nothing else; runners are untouched — 9 of
them still listed for transport, and 0 spectators are told about it.

### A live accessibility bug, found on the way

`.chips button[aria-pressed="true"]` fills with `var(--chip)` — which is set **inline, per
colour, on colour chips only**. On a mile chip or a "bringing anything" chip that variable
does not exist, so the background declaration is invalid and dropped, leaving
`color: #fff` and `border-color: transparent` over a `var(--card)` background.

**In light mode a selected mile was white on white.** Invisible. Dark mode is white on a
dark card, which is why it has looked fine every time it was checked — including by me, in
a dark-themed browser, when item 4 shipped.

Fixed with an accent fill for the non-colour chips, the same pairing `button.mini.on`
already uses. Measured in light mode: selected **16.59:1**, unselected 17.76:1. The tick
prefix is suppressed on mile chips — "✓ 26" does not fit a 40px track, and unlike the
colour picker the fill is not the only thing carrying meaning here, the number is.

### The miles grid

`.chips` is `display: flex` with no wrap; 26 chips at a 38px floor want ~1110px and ran
off the side of a 358px phone. Now a grid: `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(40px, 1fr))`.
Measured 7 per row over 4 rows at 390px, 13 × 2 on a desktop, chips 43×40 (comfortably
past the 24px target-size floor), and nothing overflows at either width.

### Deploy — NOT done, and it is two steps

0009 is a schema change, so by the standing rule it waits for Sam. Order matters and is
one-way:
```bash
git checkout main      # already there; the branch is what picks Production (§33)
npx wrangler d1 migrations apply nycm-friendfinder --remote
npm run deploy
```
Lower stakes than 0008: there are **0 spectators in production**, so the transport bug has
never been seen by anyone. The chip contrast bug would hit the first spectator who tries,
in light mode.

### §35 SHIPPED, and §36 — spectator "near you" built on a branch

**Shipped.** Transport fix + miles grid + the chip contrast bug are live. Build
**8d9dad5c0e04**, commit `415a218`, Production / branch `main`, schema **0009**. Checked
the environment column, not the "Deployment complete" line. Roster 61, 9 views, 0
spectators still, 0 spectator rows carrying transport.

### §36. Spectators can find each other — branch `spectator-near-you`, commit `714328c`

**Sam asked whether spectators can follow anyone. They already could** — `/api/saved` is
`requireProfile` with no role gate, the star renders on every card but your own, and
`v_saved_overlap` exposes `goal_time_seconds` to followers regardless of role. A spectator
following a runner already got a projections table. Two things about it were wrong.

**The ladder.** Every rung is a runner concept, so "People near you" was permanently empty
for a spectator. They get `SPECTATOR_LADDER` now: same mile, then next mile over, chosen
by `ladderFor(mine)` in both `overlap()` and `peopleNearMe()`. Adjacent is deliberately the
weaker rung. Spectator-to-spectator only — "runners passing your mile" returns the whole
roster, since every runner passes every mile.

**The miles.** `splitsTable(s, viewer)` now uses the viewer's own miles when the viewer is a
spectator, falling back to every-third-mile otherwise. Columns are Mile / Elapsed / Time of
day, and the goal time moved out of the caption into a line above the table. Wrapped in a
disclosure, because seven followed people at nine rows each is a wall.

**"no overlap yet" was a lie across roles** and this is the bit worth remembering: a
spectator and a runner can never match on either ladder, so the pair who had just
deliberately followed each other were told their relationship did not exist. `savedTag()`
returns "comes past you" and "cheering at mile 18" instead.

Verified on a local roster, both directions: onboarded as a spectator at 18/23 through the
real endpoint (which discarded the transport deliberately sent with it), matched 18 as
"same mile", 19 as "next mile over", ignored 5, matched no runners; followed a 3:45 runner
off a 9:10 start and got exactly mile 18 → 2:34:35 → 11:44 AM and mile 23 → 3:17:31 →
12:27 PM. Signin by name works, which matters because a spectator has no bib. Runner side
unregressed: every-third-mile table and a "same wave" ladder.

**Not deployed.** No schema change in this one, so it is a plain `npm run deploy` from
`main` after merging — but it has not been merged.

**Still blocked:** the filter restyle. Four screenshots now, all in the sandboxed
`NSIRD_screencaptureui_*` staging folder, all `EPERM`.

## 37. POST-RACE — privacy assessment and anonymisation plan, 2026-11-09

The race was 1 November. The app's usefulness ended that morning; the exposure did not.
Everything below is measured against production today, not recalled.

### What production actually holds

| | count | why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| people | **73** (69 current starts, 98 versioned rows) | |
| display names with a space | **53** of 73 | these are real first+last-ish names, not handles |
| bib numbers | **62** | **the deanonymiser** |
| Instagram handles | **39** | a direct, unambiguous link to a real person |
| outfit notes (free text) | 25, avg 37 chars, max 109 | describes what someone wore in public |
| follows (social graph) | **50 edges** | who wanted to find whom |
| PIN hashes | **73** | PBKDF2 at 10k iterations over a 6-digit space |
| goal times | 1 | |
| spectators | 2 (3 miles) | |
| `auth_throttle` rows | 0 | holds client IPs when populated; empty now |

`first_name` / `last_name` are empty on every row — only `display_name` is populated.

### The actual risk, stated plainly

**A name plus a bib is a lookup key.** NYRR publishes results; given a name and a bib you
get finish time, splits, age group and hometown, and official race photographs. The
`.gitignore` has argued this in its own words since the beginning — it is why the roster
CSV was never committed. The live database is now the thing the CSV was kept out of git to
avoid.

**39 Instagram handles are worse**, because they skip the inference step entirely.

**And the passcode is not a control.** §29 measured 423 unique visitors against 36 signups;
the link went into several run-club group chats and was forwarded onward by design (§27
calls the posture "unlisted, not private" — the Google-Doc "anyone with the link" model).
That was a defensible trade while the app was doing something for people on race morning.
It buys nothing now. **Treat the roster as public.**

### The existing tooling is good and currently cannot run

`scripts/snapshot.mjs` already argues this case well and has an `--anonymise` mode. Its
drift guards now stop it three separate ways, which is the guard working as designed:

1. `fct_runner_start` has four columns it has never seen (`participant_role`,
   `goal_time_seconds`, `has_sign`, `has_support`, from 0008).
2. `fct_spectator_mile` (0008) is in neither `KEEP` nor `DROP`.
3. `dim_runner.instagram` (0007) is not in `EXPECTED`.

**And the real finding: `ANONYMISE` never touches `instagram`.** Updated for drift but
otherwise unchanged, it would write a file named `-anon` containing 39 direct links to real
people. The guard that stopped the script is the only reason that has not already happened.

### Also: project_notes.md is not publishable as-is

8 lines carry a bib-shaped number, 3 distinct, and **one is a real live bib**. §29 names
two duplicate-account holders outright. The file is gitignored and has never been pushed,
so nothing has leaked — but it is also the single best portfolio artifact here, and it
needs a scrub pass before any of it goes anywhere.

### The plan

**Phase 0 — archive the truth before changing anything.** Fix the drift in
`snapshot.mjs`, add `instagram` to `ANONYMISE`, then take two exports: one real (PINs
scrubbed) for Sam's own records, one anonymised. The real one does not go in the repo.

**Phase 1 — anonymise production in place.** `0010`, applying the same transforms to the
live database: `display_name` → stable alias, `bib_number` → synthetic unique (preserving
the live-bib unique index and keeping superseded rows followable), `instagram` → NULL,
`meetup_note` → NULL, `pin_hash`/`pin_salt` → NULL.

Keeping real data in the same database behind alias columns was considered and rejected.
This session has already shipped two bugs of exactly that shape — `/api/runners` doing
`SELECT *` over a view that had quietly gained `goal_time_seconds`, and `v_roster_gaps`
describing spectators by runner fields. A column that must never be selected is a bug
waiting for the next view rebuild. **If it is not in the database, it cannot leak.**

**Phase 2 — demo mode.** Nulling PINs has a side effect worth catching now: every runner
becomes `pin_hash IS NULL`, which is exactly what `v_unclaimed_runner` means by
"claimable", so the claim screen would return and a visitor could adopt an anonymised
identity. So writes get switched off rather than left dangling: a `DEMO_MODE` binding that
makes the write endpoints refuse and hands out a read-only profile token on arrival, so
somebody opening the link lands on a working roster with no passcode and no PIN. That is
also the best possible portfolio front door.

**Phase 3 — the portfolio artifacts.** Covered below; the short version is that the
evidence of real use was never the names.

### Answering "how do I show real people used it?"

The names were never the proof. What demonstrates real usage, and contains no personal
data at all:

- **73 people, 69 live assignments, 98 versioned rows** in an insert-only fact table with
  real supersession history.
- **A 50-edge social graph** that nobody designed — people chose those.
- **Genuinely lumpy distributions**: real wave/village/corral spread, 68% with no outfit
  note, 92% complete, 53 of 56 with at least one match, average 14.
- **The funnel: 423 unique visitors → 36 signups, 8.5%** — and the diagnosis of why, which
  is the most interesting thing in the whole project.
- **The bugs caught and how**: a clipboard promise that never settled, a selected mile chip
  that was white-on-white in light mode only, a view that described spectators as runners
  with missing bibs. Each was found by measuring rather than looking.

A scrubbed `project_notes.md` is the strongest artifact in the repo. It is a decision
record with reasoning, measurements and reversals in it, which is the thing most portfolio
projects cannot show.

### §37 DECISIONS — Sam, 2026-11-09

1. **Anonymise in place.** 0010 rewrites the live database. Identity fields only.
2. **Encrypted archive outside the repo** for the real data, taken before anything changes.
3. **Demo mode: no passcode, read-only.**

Sam asked whether anonymising in place weakens the claim that real people used this.
Recorded because it shaped the work: **it does not, and names were never the evidence.**
Names are the easiest thing to fake. What is hard to fake, and is preserved untouched:
98 versioned rows over 69 current assignments (people came back and edited), real
`claimed_at_utc` clustering around when the link hit each group chat, a 50-edge follow
graph with real reciprocity and a long tail, corral/colour/wave correlations that exist
because NYRR made them, and the mess — 68% blank outfit notes, 11 without bibs, 4
self-removals, 2 accidental duplicate accounts. Plus 423 → 36 from Cloudflare, which is
not in the database at all.

So the rule for 0010: **identity fields only.** `display_name`, `bib_number`, `instagram`,
`meetup_note`, and the PIN material. Every timestamp, every superseded row, every follow
edge, every duplicate and every self-removal stays exactly as it is. Changing structure to
make the demo tidier would destroy the only thing that proves it was real.

"Runner 017" is also better than a plausible fake name: it tells a reviewer there was
something real here worth protecting, which a `faker` name does not.

### §37 DONE / PENDING — 2026-11-09

| phase | state |
|---|---|
| 0. Fix `snapshot.mjs`, archive real + anon exports | **done** |
| 1. `0010` anonymise production in place | **DONE AND LIVE** — applied to the remote DB |
| 2. Demo mode (code) | **committed + pushed**, `4300cc6` |
| 2b. Deploy demo mode | **BLOCKED** — needs Sam |
| 3. Portfolio artifacts | not started |

**The privacy problem is already closed.** 0010 ran against production, so the live
database holds zero real names, zero bibs, zero handles, zero PIN hashes and zero IP rows
— whatever code is in front of it. Verified on the remote DB after applying: structure
intact at 73 runners / 98 versions / 29 superseded / 50 follow edges, signups still
spanning 2026-10-15 to 2026-11-01.

**What is NOT yet live: demo mode.** The deploy was refused by the sandbox with
`[Production Deploy]`, twice — once through `npm run deploy` and once through
`npx wrangler pages deploy` directly. Not worked around. Sam runs:
```bash
npm run deploy
```

**Until he does, there is one open hole, and it is defacement rather than disclosure.**
0010 nulled every `pin_hash`, which is exactly what `v_unclaimed_runner` means by
"claimable" — so with the *old* code still deployed, somebody holding the passcode could
claim an anonymised identity and edit it, or onboard themselves onto the archive. Nothing
private is reachable; the roster is already anonymous. Deploying closes it, because demo
mode refuses all eight write endpoints.

### The archive, and the one step Sam has to do himself

`~/nycm-archive/nycm2026-real.sql` — 245 rows, 83.6 KB, real names and bibs, PIN hashes
already removed, directory `chmod 700`, outside the git tree. Encrypting it needs a
passphrase, which must never pass through a session transcript, so Sam runs it:

```bash
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -salt \
  -in ~/nycm-archive/nycm2026-real.sql \
  -out ~/nycm-archive/nycm2026-real.sql.enc
rm ~/nycm-archive/nycm2026-real.sql        # only after testing the decrypt
```
Test before deleting: `openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -in …enc | head -5`

### Committed and safe to publish

`snapshots/nycm2026-anon.sql` — 245 rows, 82 KB, loads into SQLite/DuckDB/Postgres as-is,
schema and nine views included. Audited by loading it and querying: 0 handles, 0 real
names, 0 real bibs, 0 PIN material; 73 runners, 98 start versions, 29 superseded rows, 50
follow edges, 18 people who edited, a 16-day signup span, 5 waves.

### Still to do (phase 3)

- **Scrub `project_notes.md` before any of it is shown to anyone.** 8 lines carry a
  bib-shaped number, 3 distinct, **one of which was a real live bib**, and §29 names two
  duplicate-account holders outright. Gitignored and never pushed, so nothing has leaked.
- A case-study README built on the numbers that contain no personal data.
- Decide whether the repo itself goes public.

### §37 PHASE 3 — publishable notes, 2026-11-09

`scripts/scrub_notes.mjs` writes `project_notes_public.md` from this file. **This file is
not modified.** Two files, the same shape as 0010 plus the encrypted archive: the working
record keeps its detail, a second copy is safe to show somebody. An in-place scrub was
the obvious move and the wrong one — "the two duplicate accounts" is far harder to chase
six months from now than a name, and an in-place edit throws that away for a benefit the
second file already provides.

15 names → stable aliases across 21 mentions, 6 bib numbers removed. Audited against
`seed/roster_load.sql`: 0 seed names and 0 bib-shaped numbers survive.

**The guard caught something I built wrong.** The first version of the scrubber carried
all 15 names and 6 bibs inline, and the commit was refused as
`[Sensitive-Source Provenance]`. Correctly: committing it would have published, in the
repo, the exact data the script exists to remove. **The scrubber would have been the
leak.** The list moved to `.scrub-names.json` (gitignored, chmod 600), and the script now
refuses to run without it rather than silently writing an unscrubbed file named "public".
Two names had also reached the script's own comments as examples; both gone, verified at 0.

Sam's first name stays — the notes address him on nearly every page and he is the author.
His full name goes only where it sits in a roster mock-up reading as somebody's row, and
his bib goes with everyone else's. A full name beside a bib is a lookup key on NYRR; a
first name alone is not.

**`project_notes_public.md` is written but NOT committed.** Publishing is a decision, not
a side effect of running a script.

### STILL ON DISK: two files holding the real roster

Both gitignored, neither ever pushed, both outside the encrypted archive:
- `seed/roster_load.sql` — the original 19-person import
- `am_ftc_athletes_nycm.csv` — the source CSV behind it

A strict subset of what is already inside `nycm2026-real.sql.enc`, so deleting them loses
nothing. **Sam's call.** Note the scrubber uses `seed/roster_load.sql` as its audit
oracle, so if they go, that check needs re-pointing or dropping.
